A new python-based auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) program called ipie has been created. This program is designed for use with semi-empirical and density-functional theory Hamiltonians and is particularly well-suited for parallel processing on GPU's as well as CPU and accelerator devices like NVIDIA's Tensor Core GPUs. This program's flexibility and performance have been demonstrated through a variety of tests that show it can handle a range of methods including imaginary time projection, constrained and perturbed CASSCF, and perturbation theory. These tests also demonstrate the effectiveness of ipie in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and simplicity of use. For instance, ipie was found to be able to calculate the binding energy of helium to five-digit accuracy with just a few core CPU's or a high-end GPU. Additionally, calculations of molecular dissociation energies and the ionization potential of water have been performed with ipie. These studies also compared ipie against other quantum Monte Carlo programs in terms of accuracy and found the results to be competitive even when running on much older hardware. Finally, some future studies that can be performed with ipie are discussed including the application of perturbation theory to treat correlated systems. Overall, ipie's performance and effectiveness make it a useful tool for educational and research purposes. This program is entirely open-source and can be obtained at https://github.com/mrc-2020/ipie. Further information, including documentation, examples, and results of ipie can be obtained at https://ipie-mrc.github.com. The Python 3-based ipie program has its roots in 2014 when development first began on the AFQMC method. Over time ipie has been refined and has produced many results that have been published in scientific journals. A key innovation of ipie and other python-based quantum Monte Carlo programs is its ability to be easily extended through the use of python modules as well as its native C++ code. This program's simplicity has also allowed for the creation of a number of subprograms that perform specific tasks in the quantum Monte Carlo method as well as proofs of concept for new ideas. These programs can be easily extended by others using the same techniques that were used to initially develop them, making the code as useful as possible to the community. Convergence analysis of a finite element method applied to a Stokes variational inequality is performed in the context of ice flow models in glaciology. Specifically, the common case of a prescribed contact height is examined. Due to the nature of the variational inequality as a nonlinear non-convex problem, where contact areas are dependent on velocity, a major hurdle to overcome is the absence of a continuous interpolant that respects the contact constraint. By establishing the convergence of a specific numerical scheme, which combines a hierarchical finite element method with a nonlinear iteration scheme, it is demonstrated that near-optimal rates of convergence can be achieved in the L2 norm for the gradient of the stress tensor. Critical to this outcome is the utilization of a hierarchical basis first introduced by Babuska and Prager in 1969. An additional consequence of the analysis is the confirmation of a specific decoupling effect associated with weakly-supplied boundary conditions common in glaciology, which had previously been established in a 1988 study by J. R\u{a}sz, B. Simondy, and I. T\u{a}t\'{e}. Additionally, the current work draws connections to recent findings by P. Kaplick\'{a} in 2013 regarding the continuous dependence of the stress tensor on the velocity. To facilitate a stable numerical simulation, a specific iterative scheme is employed which is informed by the theory of quasi-variations as described in a 2006 study by P. Kaplick\'{a} and M. Z\'{a}vada. A unique aspect of the presented analysis is its explicit consideration of the physical implications of the variational inequality, an approach distinct from the more abstract, generalized models prevalent in the literature. A detailed description of the nonlinear iteration scheme, replete with analytical estimates, underscores the importance of utilizing specialized techniques even in the realm of concrete physical models. Finally, a comprehensive selection of numerical examples are presented which confirm the analytical findings and provide insight into the behavior of ice bodies under various conditions. One such example involves the numerical simulation of an ice block under purely incremental loading, where a stable solution is demonstrated using the presented iterative scheme. A second example, however, reveals the occurrence of squeezing in the case of abrupt, instantaneous loading, where a stable solution is ultimately achieved albeit via a long and sometimes unstable nonlinear iteration history. A thorough analysis of these numerical examples, expressed in terms of both quantitative results and a qualitative discussion, enables the derivation of a heuristic criterion for predicting the occurrence of squeezing

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable data and resources. Pre-training on vast datasets can significantly improve performance by leveraging rich unsupervised information. Golf cart image datasets offer an abundance of unlabelled data due to their low resolution and vast availability. Research indicates that depth estimation can provide better pre-training than traditional classification tasks. However, it remains unclear if depth estimates from low-resolution or high-resolution images are more beneficial. We compared the effectiveness of various forms of pre-training for semantic segmentation, including classification and depth estimation at both high and low resolutions. Contrary to our expectation, we found that depth estimates from low-resolution images were more beneficial than those from high-resolution images and offered superior results compared to classification-based pre-training. Moreover, by reapplying a decoder designed for depth estimation, we were able to enhance the performance of the baseline classifier. These findings highlight the significance of depth estimation as a means of pre-training for semantic segmentation tasks on golf cart image datasets. This research investigates the optimal radius of equivalence for function series that meet certain criteria related to log-harmonic mappings in the complex plane. Specifically, we consider functions that preserve a certain geometric structure and their corresponding logarithmic derivatives, where the relationship between these properties is characterized by a geometric constraint. By establishing a key statement describing the relationship between these conditions, we derive a measure for the radius of equivalence in the set of such functions and provide supporting examples of this theorem. Additionally, we define a geometrically inspired notion of Bohr's radius and demonstrate its applicability to specific families of functions that satisfy additional harmonic mean value conditions. This investigation also employs graphical methods to visualize and validate the results of this theorem. Ultimately, we utilize our findings to derive a corresponding result for a specific class of multivariate functions that satisfy additional geometric criteria. In contrast to many predator-prey models based on Holling-Tanner's predator response type, our study introduces a novel variation that incorporates an Allee effect into prey population growth, resulting in a model that differs from the standard HT model. The new model's equilibrium points and associated stability properties are analyzed, as well as the occurrence and nature of nonlinearity-driven bifurcations triggered by the Allee behavior in prey populations. Specifically, this study examines coherent bifurcations and Hopf bifurcations alongside their respective bifurcation and saddle-node homoclinic bifurcations. Furthermore, our investigation into periodic orbits focuses on their persistence, stability, and global structure, with the confirmation that, in fact, all possible periodic orbits do indeed exist within this model. Lastly, our work also explores and illustrates the potential co-occurrence of Allee behavior, limit cycles, and oscillatory patterns in predator and prey populations, thereby providing insights into possible predator-prey dynamics when considering these ecological species. The analyzed dynamics are particularly relevant to numerous real-world predator-prey systems. The studied model is particularly apt for describing complex interactions between two species: the predator, which exhibits a type II response, and the prey, which experiences an Allee effect due to limitations in resources availability. Such a scenario can be observed in many examples, such as real data sets describing the zooplankton-pelagic fish interaction in the Lake Constance. Therefore, our research not only contributes to a deeper understanding of these ecological systems but also offers recommendations for future observations and experiments. This paper builds upon previous work by Bisseling regarding the Aspect Pivot Simplex (APS) technique for linear programming, specifically focusing on the linear iteration limit aspect. Initially, a crucial concept under the APS umbrella is established - the index path - and its effectiveness in generating feasible indices within the APS framework is demonstrated through the application of a principle similar to the strong citizenship property. Furthermore, this achievement is utilized to establish a principle for the creation of positive rays within the APS, thereby facilitating the determination of a feasible solution when the APS is at a linear iteration limit. Ultimately, this study illustrates that by implementing the obtained principles consistently, the APS can terminate after determining the first feasible point, achieving a substantial computational efficiency gain. Interestingly, empirical experiments revealed that the newly established principles can, in some cases, cause the APS to conclude even faster than the currently implemented algorithms can, although a comprehensive analysis of this finding remains out of the scope of this study. Nonetheless, preliminary observations suggest that the concept of the index path possesses the potential to significantly impact the current understanding of linear programming. An additional paper will explore the second key aspect of the APS - the simplex jump - in greater detail.

This paper undertakes a detailed examination of the influence of off-shell charm and bottom quark contributions on top quark mass (tsm) measurement in events involving ttj production at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Utilizing the full matrix element information for ttj processes, and incorporating a next-to-leading order (NLO) correction along with a multiple-channel fitting approach to account for finite and infinite duration effects of unstable quarks, a comprehensive calculation is achieved. In this calculation, tsm measurements in dileptonic standard model (SM) ttj events are compared with those obtained from dileptonic dilepton channels in both SM and in presence of a weakly interacting dark matter (wIMD) scenario, with the later involving an off-shell contribution from a charmed quark. Our results indicate that, even with the presence of a large laboratory frame energy and slight departure from its benchmark value, a reliable tsm measurement can be obtained even when considering just the on-shell contribution. Though the off-shell correction has a minor impact on its accuracy, it is however essential for precise measurements. By comparing the outcomes with those obtained from a partial width extraction in dileptonic dilepton channels, we see that the former provides better precision here as well. Lastly, through a simulation of a real LHC experiment with a dataset of 300 fb^-1, we test the sensitivity of the ttj production to various properties of a dark matter (DM) candidate spanning a considerable range of masses and annihilation cross-sections. Our examination reveals that the former primarily determines the value of tsm while the latter influences the mass of the dark matter candidate, with detection being possible in such an LHC scenario with a very high degree of certainty. With the presence of a large number of such events in ttj production at the LHC, a precise measurement of tsm along with detection of wIMD in a wide variety of scenarios including this one is expected. This, in turn, provides a potential means to distinguish between different types of quark properties with very high degree of certainty. Many Evolutionary Algorithms are designed to run in parallel, but their asynchronous nature can cause problems because they're often scored at random intervals. Several solutions aim to improve performance by dividing the population and evaluating different parts at set times, but these approaches can lead to uneven development and slow healing if a member's evaluation is delayed. To address this, a new method called FPSE creates a parental selection process that's centered around evaluation times, allowing the best candidates to be identified and utilized immediately. This algorithm divides the population into groups based on evaluation times and places the best members from each group at the top of the population ranking, giving them a higher chance of being selected for the next generation. Experiments confirm that FPSE helps reduce the effect of delayed evaluation and promotes a more balanced population. When compared to traditional Parallel Evolutionary Algorithms, FPSE achieves better performance overall and significantly reduces the time it takes to converge. However, FPSE relies on accurate estimates of the evaluation times and requires a mechanism to handle changes in those times. While achieving optimal performance is complex, FPSE delivers consistent results and promotes a more stable evolutionary process. Several strategies, such as dividing the population and using replacement methods, are proposed to further improve FPSE, with more extensive research needed to explore these directions. The paper concludes that FPSE demonstrates promising performance and stability, making it a reliable tool for understanding the impact of asynchronous evaluations on Multi-objective Evolutionary Algorithms. By accounting for evaluation time variability, FPSE provides a foundation for developing more precise models of parallel evolutionary processes. To fill a notable knowledge gap, more comprehensive studies are needed to delve into the intricacies of evaluation time modeling and their influence on MOEA behavior. The paper's results open the door for an original follow-up study, inviting the reader to join the investigation. Initially, it's essential to expand FPSE to simulate a broad spectrum of evaluation time distributions, followed by developing methods for estimating evaluation times and creating adaptive mechanisms to balance population growth. Research could also involve embedding FPSE within a more general framework, allowing for analysis of various Multi-objective Evolutionary Algorithms through modeling and simulation. The primary goal of such a framework would be to uncover the underlying principles of asynchronous evolutionary processes with the long-term aim of developing a generalized theory for optimizing Multi-objective Evolutionary Algorithms at all scales. To confirm FPSE's potential as a research tool, it would be necessary to conduct a series of experiments designed to investigate and validate its underlying principles, effectively paving the way for its widespread adoption in understanding the mechanics of evolutionary processes

Many physical systems exhibit periodic behavior tied to a specific time interval, $T$. In many cases, the evolution of these systems over a time interval that is a multiple of $T$, $\tau=NT$, where $N$ is an integer, can be accurately described using a simplified, high-precision approximation that takes into account the original complex dynamics. This simplified description takes the form of a time-independent, Hermitian operator and provides a complete and accurate representation of the original time-dependent, non-Hermitian dynamics for all values of $N$. Reference [1] outlines a universal method for creating these accurate approximations for any given $N$, and in this study, a computationally efficient approach is developed that simplifies the high-rate expansion for systems that are oscillatory in time but non-Hermitian. This simplification is based on a new identity that separates the original dynamics into a time-dependent, Hermitian part and a time-independent, non-Hermitian part, and it allows for the creation of simplified, high-precision approximations that are similar to those found in [1]. These approximations are exact to a certain order of $1/T$ and capture key aspects of the original dynamics, and they can be used to identify important characteristics, such as resonant frequencies and times, that play a crucial role in the behavior of the system. This approach is demonstrated using two systems that are known to be oscillatory in time but non-Hermitian: a quantum oscillator that loses energy, and a quantum oscillator that interacts with a quadratic bath, and in each case, the high-rate expansion is simplified using the new time decomposition identity. These simplifications reveal new and insightful properties that are relevant at all times, and they can be used to create very accurate approximations that are useful for a wide range of values of $N$. These approximations are expressed in terms of powers of $1/T$ and contain a series of corrections that can be calculated in a step-by-step manner. Each correction to the approximation captures an increasingly small aspect of the original dynamics, and it allows for a highly accurate representation of the original time-dependent, non-Hermitian dynamics for any given $N$. This accurate approximation can be used to create new and insightful metrics that are relevant at all times, and it provides a complete and systematic approach to creating high-rate expansions for time-oscillating, non-Hermitian generators. These approximations are applicable to a wide range of physical systems that are oscillatory in time

The formation of massive stars is a key aspect of research in the field of star formation.  A critical factor in the early mass-loss process associated with these massive stars is the slow and massive wind, which creates opportunities for the interstellar medium to cool. High velocity dispersion and broad lines are characteristic of massive star environments, but there is limited understanding of how these phenomena interact with the interstellar medium to facilitate cooling mechanisms. To investigate this interaction, researchers examined 21 cm lines observed by the STRONGER survey, focusing on particular regions with narrow and broad spectral components, as well as a previously unexplored region near the massive star-forming region G176.51+00.20. The data revealed the presence of self-absorption in 21 cm lines, which may indicate the emergence of dense gas from the slow massive wind of a high-mass star. Researchers hypothesize that these dense gas regions could be the initial points of molecular condensation and proto-star formation. 

Given the significant differences in the properties of massive star environments and proto-star formation regions, the detection of dense gas in the massive star-forming region G176.51+00.20 holds important implications. It suggests the potential for cool gas to form and massive star formation to occur within these regions. However, to further understand this relationship, additional observations are required to determine the characteristics of these dense gas regions and whether they precede or coincide with the formation of stars. 

By studying the interactions between massive stars and the interstellar medium, researchers aim to clarify the early mass-loss process associated with these stars. 

The presence of dense gas in the region G176.51+00.20, detected through 21 cm lines, may indicate that massive star environments offer a unique platform for the creation of gas condensation sites and potential proto-star formations. 

Researchers note that more studies are necessary to firmly link the dense gas detected in this research to the formation of stars. 

Notably, the dense gas in the region G176.51+00.20 may represent an additional pathway for the creation of gas condensation sites beyond the previously acknowledged role of ambient gas as a primary source of star-forming regions. 

Researchers aim to further investigate the complex relationships between massive stars, interstellar gas, and star formation. 

By studying these interactions, researchers aim to expand our current understanding of how massive stars form. 

The coexistence of dense gas and fast and slow winds in the region G176.51+00.20 may indicate a unique star-forming environment

We provide detailed counts for combinations of arcs in the affine plane $\mathbb F_q^2$, 
comparing them to Grassmannian varieties via polynomial sums, 
and also offer a formula for the sum of arc points, 
all within the framework of $\mathbb F_q$ geometry. 
These counts are specific cases of a broader theorem. 
The approach involves transforming arc enumerations into determinantal counts, 
a concept derived from Kapranis--Poulakis theory on non-linear hyperplane arrangements. 
The result is-enlightening, as arc counts appear as lower-dimensional analogs 
of Kapranis--Poulakis counts for rational curves. 
Additionally, accompanying evidence is given for a conjecture regarding arc enumerations. 
The methodology is tailored for $q\le 3$ and the proof is fully presented for $q=2$. 
For $q=4$, only the enumerations are provided due to computational complexity. 
Lastly, the problem of finding higher-degree analogs for arc enumerations is proposed. 
It is suspected that such an expression would be infeasible for arcs of degree greater than one. 
To support this, attempts to prove the conjecture for arcs of the second degree are presented. 
The first involves a straightforward approach, and the second utilizes Galois theory. 
Regrettably, these attempts were unsuccessful. 
It is hypothesized, therefore, that a computable formula for arc enumerations 
for arcs of the second degree might not be achievable. 
To conclude, a number of open problems and directions for future research are presented. 
The most challenging of these is to achieve a complete enumeration of smooth intersections 
of high-degree curves, a goal that has eluded researchers for decades. 
It is hoped, therefore, that a formula for such intersections might be 
realized as part of a broader system for enumerating smooth geometric objects.

who contribute to these problems for $q\ge 5$ might 
achieve a solution, and the associated code can be accessed at

This research aims to design a more effective visualization tool that demonstrates all six possible cases of triangle congruence without relying on 'aesthetic' diagrams, which can mislead students. To gain insights into its development and composition, we investigated the cluster's distribution of Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect (SZE) and gas temperature, as well as its dark matter distribution, using archival data. Our analysis indicates that the cluster possesses two distinct gas components - a hotter, outer layer and a cooler, central region - that likely corresponds to the differing SZE signals observed in the east and west clusters. These distinct components may contribute to the formation of the large-scale radio halo. Furthermore, we found that the cluster's temperature distribution does not exhibit any unusual features. Using a previously observed X-ray map, we determined the SZE flux to be primarily inscribed in the larger, cooler eastern component. These findings are consistent with the system undergoing a dynamic process, where the larger, eastern component may have recently interacted with the smaller, western cluster. It is also plausible that the unique SZE profile is a result of a jet that originated from an active galactic nucleus within a galaxy located within the larger, eastern component. Additional, in-depth studies are required to thoroughly examine this intriguing system.

Through thorough experiments and analysis, this research identifies and overcomes specific challenges associated with parallelization and adapts existing optimization techniques to optimize LMMS performance on modern GPUs. This optimization breakthrough enables the potential for low-latency LMMS-based intelligence in robotics, vision, and other complex perception and control systems. By introducing a new learning rule and allowing agents to move freely, our simulations show that a stable language system can develop, where multiple words represent a single concept, and new concepts emerge as a result of social connections. Research into physics-informed neural networks for solving partial differential equations has shown that imposing regularization on the neural network's output can provide a more accurate solution when a sufficient amount of data is not available. This study aims to investigate another regularization method that utilizes the momentum term to counter increased oscillations in the network's momenta during the optimization process. As these oscillations can trigger the extraction of general lessons from the data, the momentum term offers a promising regularization method. This study demonstrates that introducing a momentum term in physics-informed neural networks can mitigate the effects of spectral bias, leading to improved generalization performance when training these networks. This improved performance also results in reduced runtimes, as smaller networks require less computational time to train. These benefits come with some limitations, including increased optimization difficulty and reduced convergence rates, which can be mitigated by incorporating a penalty term into the loss function. This study provides an overview of the theory behind this regularization method and supports it with numerical results that show improved generalization performance and reduced computational costs in a variety of PDE-based applications. These results also illustrate the potential to adapt this method to address specific challenges, such as handling multiple targets, providing initial/boundary conditions, and solving non-smooth PDE systems. This research is expected to facilitate the development of more resilient physics-informed neural networks, allowing them to accurately solve a broader range of partial differential equations. Future work is recommended to address the current limitations of this method, including its decreased convergence rates, and to expand its applications to additional PDE-based problems. This research is expected to contribute to the advancement of deep learning methods for partial differential equations, leading to improved accuracy, efficiency, and stability. These wave equations are dampened by a Kelvin-Voigt type of friction, but with the constant typically replaced with a spatially varying function. Using the finite element method, we explore the impact of replacing the constant with a spatially varying function and find that the resulting models lose their natural stability properties. Nevertheless, we are able to prove the existence of stable solutions for infinite amounts of time by replacing the constant with a carefully controlled, spatially varying function that slows down down the transfer of energy, effectively creating a filter effect. Typically, agents either develop their policies through trial and error or adopt rule-based approaches with pre-defined rules.  We propose a new method that combines the advantages of both frames of work by using a hierarchical reinforcement learning model. The highest level of this framework represents broad goals, while lower levels focus on specific subtasks.  To implement this, we suggest an integrated framework that integrates reinforcement learning and inductive logic programming, allowing the translation of state information to logic atomic predicates and the generation of abstract subtasks from observed observations.  Within our framework, the reinforcement learning module develops general goals, while the inductive learning module defines abstract subtasks, and a controller module selects specific subtasks based on goal conditions.  We illustrate the efficacy of our approach using a complex real-world problem, namely the control of a HurriCube prototype with impaired Robin sonar capabilities, demonstrating that our method allows for the simultaneous optimization of both mission objectives and subtask specifics.  We demonstrate that our model is interpretable, providing insights into which factors contribute to the failure of a sonar system.  Although our method demands more computational resources, it significantly reduces the required number of experiments, as demonstrated through comparison with an unstructured reinforcement learning approach.  Our experiments showcase the potential of hierarchical reinforcement learning, highlighting its superiority over non-hierarchical methods, and the synergy between our approach and inductive logic programming sheds light on the importance of understanding the underlying world model when designing autonomous agents.  Ultimately, our method demonstrates the feasibility of inducing sparse, interpretable models that complement the learned policies, paving the way for the integration of all aspects of a domain into the learning process.  We envision our framework as a starting point for the development of other domain-agnostic transfer methods, allowing the separation of task-related factors from strategy-related factors.  Additionally, our approach provides a theoretical foundation for the transfer of knowledge between domains by distinguishing between world factors and learning factors.  Specifically, our framework highlights the key role of inductive logic programming in extracting the underlying world model, and our experimental results emphasize the importance of domain models in the context of reinforcement learning.  We further investigate the potential applications of our approach by examining its extension to other domains, such as robotic navigation and financial trading, and by exploring the connection between our method and other transfer techniques. We issue two minimax challenges inspired by Fenton's work. Firstly, for $p=2,$ we aim to find the precise minimax value over $L_2([0,T])$ for functions of the form $g(t) = \sum_{k=1}^m c_k \phi_T(t - \tau_k)$, where $\phi_T(t) = \chi_{[0,T]}(t) - \frac{T}{\sqrt{\pi}} \sin(\sqrt{\lambda_1 t})$, $\lambda_1$ is the first Dirichlet eigenvalue on $[0,T]$ and c's are real numbers. Secondly, for any $1 < p < \infty,$ we seek to determine the precise minimax value over $L_p([0,T])$ for functions of the form $g(t) = \sum_{k=1}^m c_k \phi_T(t - \tau_k)$, where the support of $\phi_T(t)$ is restricted to $[0,T]$. These problems have applications in the regularization of coefficients for one-dimensional elliptic boundary value problems.  They represent advanced versions of Fenton's original challenge, which focused on the specific case of $g(t) = c_1 \phi_T(t) + c_2 \phi_T(t - \tau_1).$ Our proof strategies differ significantly from Fenton's. They rely on the spectral decomposition of the Dirichlet Laplacian and involve intricate arguments on the almost everywhere convergence of series of eigenfunctions in $L_p$ spaces for $1 < p < \infty.$ The work will be extended to higher-dimensional cases in a subsequent paper. Formal verification is crucial, but current methods face the challenges of natural language specification and program encoding, which are unsustainable for complex systems.  We aim to overcome these obstacles by adopting a new approach that directly leverages linguistic structures, such as phrase structure grammar, to generate Hoare axioms automatically.  We have developed a method that translates a domain-specific language into Hoare logic, leveraging the power of linguistic structures to fragment the program's domain, thus facilitating its formalization.  This method has been demonstrated with two case studies, including a proof assistant's specification and a phrase-based description of the merge sort algorithm, which were automatically translated into Hoare axioms and employed for the merge sort program verification.  We observed a substantial increase in the size of the programs that could be formally verified without encoding them into predicate logic, from 1-10 levels, compared to the traditional approach that requires manual encoding and is typically limited to levels of 2-3.  We also observed a considerable reduction in the fragmentation of the program domain, from 512 to 281 subdomains.  This breakthrough allows for the formal verification of programs with more complex specifications without encoding them into predicate logic.  We tested our method against various program fragments from a verified library and the merge sort algorithm, successfully verifying eight programs across 10 specifications without manual intervention.  Combining Hoare logic with phrase structure grammar yields an enhanced compositional semantics, signifying a fundamental improvement.  This method offers a significant shift in program verification, addressing a long-standing challenge of incorporating natural language specification and program encoding difficulties.  It has important implications for the development of a natural language-based proof assistant, paving the way for the formal validation of programs from logical forms of natural language specifications.  Furthermore, our technique demonstrates its practical utility by applying it to a concrete verification task, thus showcasing its potential to elevate program verification to a higher level of sophistication.  This verification task can be visualized using an interactive tool, enabling users to discover the specified program properties through interactive exploration.  Ultimately, the method's practical validity will be determined by its effectiveness in verifying increasingly complex programs with specifications.  If it fails to do so, the proposed concept of natural Hoare reasoning will remain an intriguing theoretical advancement.  To address potential limitations, the next step involves refining the current prototype Hoare logic and the associated translation rules to simplify the specification process.  If successful, this modification will have far-reaching implications for the development of a natural language-based proof assistant, making natural language an ideal specification language

Recent studies have used to quantify the bending modulus of lipid membranes, revealing an increase in modulus with cholesterol content. However, there are limitations to this method, particularly its assumption that the modulus remains consistent across different sampling methods. Analyzing phosphocholine lipid membranes, these findings suggest a cutoff point for the effect of cholesterol content at a spherical shape scale. Below this threshold, membrane composition exhibits polydispersity in molecular shape, making the modulus sensitive to dataset interpretation. Yet, at this threshold and above, the membrane transitions to a more ordered, bilayer shape with a relatively constant modulus regardless of composition. By comparing various cholesterol incorporation models and their resulting moduli, it is evident that a specific range of cholesterol content can be identified, between 20-40 mole percent, where the membrane has reached a more ordered state. This research emphasizes the need to consider the complex interactions between molecular structure and curvature when assessing mechanical properties in membrane biology. Additionally, it presents a hypothesis that a more ordered, solid-like state may be present in membranes containing high amounts of cholesterol. This can now be explained, counteracting an earlier theory that attributed increased stiffness to increased disorder within the membrane. Instead, it is clear that a specific range of cholesterol content is associated with a transition to a more ordered state. Finally, it is acknowledged that assessing mechanical properties in membrane biology is complex and multifaceted, involving both curvature and shape sensitivity. Therefore, it is essential to consider these factors when examining membrane behavior and to be cautious when interpreting results, particularly when analyzing data from various sources and sampling methods.

In machine learning, reliable uncertainty assessment is crucial for informed decision-making, particularly in real-world operations. Deep neural networks have made significant progress in object detection, but accurate uncertainty prediction remains a major challenge, primarily due to the reliance of post-processing methods on the unreliable class probabilities provided by the model. We introduce an innovative approach, BayesOD, which redefines uncertainty assessment for object detection by framing it as a latent data issue using Bayesian inference. This method incorporates uncertainty propagation into the model's forward pipeline, enabling uncertainty information to be retained in the model's output. We also develop a novel uncertainty evaluation, tailored for object detection, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through both subjective and objective evaluations on the COCO dataset. The source code for BayesOD has been made publicly available on the GitHub platform. The model's performance is visualized in an accompanying video. 

Results on the COCO dataset demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in both objective and subjective evaluations. Specifically, it significantly excels in the detection of difficult samples (with an area under the ROC curve of 85.97% compared to 82.72% for ACOP) and accurately estimates its own uncertainties (with a mean absolute error of 9.97% compared to 12.85% for the class-based uncertainty method). Moreover, our approach effectively propagates uncertainty to specific object regions (with a mean IoU of 43.25% for the easy case and 16.85% for the difficult case), outperforming the baseline models. 

We anticipate that our technique will contribute to the advancement of model uncertainty assessment for object detection and facilitate its practical application in related domains. The model's performance is visualized in an accompanying video. 

The performance of our approach is visually illustrated through a study which examines its ability to assess uncertainty during novel object detection. Specifically, we observe that the model accurately identifies its lack of knowledge about the'skateboard' class, relying instead on the related 'longboard" class due to the absence of prior knowledge regarding the detected object (with a high degree of confidence for the 'longboard" prediction). This showcases the effective propagation of uncertainty information retained in the model's output. 

We conduct an additional subjective evaluation to further investigate the performance of our approach, analyzing responses from multiple experts. The results reveal that our technique effectively assess uncertainty both at the object class and spatial levels.

In quantum phenomenon known as the pigeonhole effect, the principle holds that at least two particles out of n particles must occupy the same state. Typically, explanations for this effect rely on the use of wave functions, however, this requires highly overlapping particle distributions. We have demonstrated that the pigeonhole effect can occur with minimally overlapping particle trajectories in a two-dimensional scattering experiment involving a complex phase object. Our findings reveal that the phenomenon can be attributed to the conversion of transversal beam modes into a differential translational motion of output beams. Utilizing a simple, yet intuitive model based on the description of transversal beam modes as carrying waves with different translational displacements, we have analytically derived the probability for the occurrence of the pigeonhole effect. Furthermore, our results also highlight the difficulties in accurately describing certain phenomena using the framework of non-overlapping wave functions. The experiment described has been performed using 6 particle beams that interacted with a 1000-fold (in units of wavelength) thick carbon foil. Our results confirm that the pigeonhole effect occurs regardless of the low probability of overlapping particle trajectories. Moreover, our experiment also confirms the occurrence of a phenomenon known as the Mach-Zehnder interferometer, even with minimally overlapping particle trajectories. Our findings indicate that testing these fundamental quantum phenomenon through experiments on separable states may provide valuable insights into their physical occurrence. The method employed in our experiment can be applied to testing the pigeonhole effect using particle beams with lower energy (tens of keV) and particle distributions. Another method aimed at preserving privacy in a matrix's low-rank nature, but the result wasn't differentially private in its own right. The Lights Out game is a well-known problem that can be played on any transitive graph, typically played on a grid of size n x n. The game's objective is to switch off all lights with minimal clicks, but a longstanding challenge, first introduced by Stephen Cole Kleene, has remained unsolved for over sixty years. The maximum clicks problem - determining the maximum number of clicks needed to turn off all lights - has been a subject of inquiry since its inception. The maximum clicks dilemma, coined by Michael Attenborough, poses a question - whether this maximum clicks number ever changes as the size of the grid increases. This would mean that the number of clicks required to turn off all lights in a grid of size n x n (with the standard constraints) can either consistently equal n^2 or consistently exceed n^2, as n grows larger.

In 2017, Michael Attenborough began examining this concept more deeply, later releasing a follow-up document in 2020. Building upon his initial findings, Attenborough hypothesized that the variability in the number of clicks, denoted as delta(n), is influenced by a particular mathematical equation - n^2 - 2n - 2. With the support of computational model testing, he suggested this could be a reliable formula. The current research undertakes a fresh examination of the clicks problem through the development of new tests aimed at verifying Attenborough's hypothesis about the variability in the number of clicks and his conjecture concerning the number clicks dilemma. The research delves into the limits of the clicks problem, exploring non-standard games and identifying patterns that might shed light on the problem. The researchers tested Attenborough's hypothesis using multiple tests, confirming it to be correct but also revealing that the clicks problem can exhibit a variety of behaviors, such as the clicks dilemma itself, which is observed in a particular type of grid - those with odd sizes - where the number of clicks can either exceed the minimum possible number by one. The researchers also identified a natural extension or variation of the clicks problem, which has the potential to yield further insights into its solution. The problem, denoted as the variable sequence variant, involves making sure that the sequence of lights is switched off in a predetermined order. In graph fair learning, the goal is to develop models that are unbiased towards certain characteristics without making broad assumptions about the data distribution, which is often the case when training on diverse, representative data. However, working with multiple potential bias sources while maintaining data-specific insights can be computationally expensive due to the need for extensive training on each dataset. To solve this problem, we introduce a novel concept called "localized fairness" which focuses on minimizing bias within localized data groups (i.e., nodes with similar attributes) without requiring comprehensive retraining on each dataset. To achieve this, we formulate the localization of bias as a graph-based learning problem where the goal is to balance group-level fairness while maintaining global model performance, resulting in a mixed-norm optimization challenge that we resolve using an innovative alternative optimization algorithm. We provide a comprehensive theoretical foundation for our approach, confirming its effectiveness in enforcing fairness at the localized level without compromising model performance in various settings. Moreover, our experimental results demonstrate the practical benefits of our method by achieving better fairness-m Accuracy tradeoffs compared to existing graph fair learning techniques. To enable scalable deployment, we also propose a dimensionality-reduced graph visualization technique that effectively balances visualization clarity and model performance, preserving key characteristics of node attributes without introducing noise. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using real-world datasets such as Adult, CompCar, and Facebook Open Graph Application. The implementation of our method is available under an open-source license at https://github.com/dhilipsajjan/localfair. For interactive visualizations of our approach in action, visitors can access https://dhilipsajjan.github.io/localfair.

This study employs the methods of asymptotic analysis in a linear equation describing reversible enzyme processes. The obtained approximations are successively evaluated at lower orders, yielding an iterative sequence of solutions that converges to a fundamental solution of the original equation. The convergence is proven using a metric on the space of analytical functions. The process can be expanded to non-linear kinetic equations, provided a suitable linear approximation exists. The principle behind this approach is a geometric interpretation of differential equations as equations of curves in multi-dimensional space. The iterative solution corresponds to successively fitting curve segments. When these segments are individually geometrically meaningful, the iteration is analogous to a regularization method. The application of this approach to linear equation (1) is demonstrated for a reversible Michaelis-Menten kinetic equation and equation (2) with additional terms representing enzyme inhibition and vebose derivation is provided. The derived iterations are verified by numerical simulation using programming language Julia, which is known for its high performance in scientific computing. The numerical results confirm the convergence of the iterative sequence to a stable solution. The predicted values of bound enzyme and substrate concentrations exhibit significant stability at iterations beyond 3. The inclusion of inhibition in the model also demonstrates converged values for bound enzyme and substrate concentrations and product concentrations at iterations beyond 4. The numerical results for both models show good agreement with known experimental data. The proposed method is a valuable tool for solving kinetic equations in scientific research. This study employed the Feynman-path-integral method to examine the behavior of a driven quantum harmonic oscillator. However, due to the oscillator's nonlinear phase factor in the path integral, which prevents a direct analytical solution, the Markov-Chain Monte-Carlo method was utilized to sample the oscillator's trajectories and derive numerical approximations of observable values. Two distinct algorithms were explored: the Unadjusted Langevin Metropolis and the Malinin algorithms, with the latter incorporating a novel adaptation of the Metropolis-hastings technique that incorporates virtual wall techniques to improve acceptance rates. Our findings indicate that the Malinin algorithm yields more accurate results than the Unadjusted Langevin Metropolis algorithm, and that both methods are suitable for simulating the oscillator's behavior. Additionally, the Unadjusted Langevin Metropolis algorithm may be applied to systems requiring periodic boundary conditions in the future. Calculations of spectral densities using the Malinin algorithm demonstrated convergence towards known limiting expressions for underdamped oscillators, and suggested that applying this method to the harmonic oscillator could be extended to broader classes of quantum systems. Lastly, a companion code implementing the Unadjusted Langevin Metropolis and Malinin algorithms is provided in the JULIA language (Julia v1.6). Due to the Unadjusted Langevin Metropolis algorithm's relatively straightforward logic, it is feasible that this code could be adapted for applications in multiple programming languages. Nonetheless, the Malinin algorithm, which involves a relatively more intricate set of logic, may require significant reformulation before it can be effectively applied in other programming languages. Still, based on our experience, the Julia code provides a well-structured foundation for future development. Review-based product recommendations have become increasingly crucial in enhancing user experience and the overall quality of service. However, traditional recommendation methods that solely considered rating information were ineffective when dealing with negative reviews from satisfied customers. To overcome this limitation, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN) that utilizes review texts and their corresponding ratings in a more intelligent manner. The proposed framework consists of two key components: (i) A review embedding module that interacts with ratings to better understand review content. (ii) A rating forecasting module that estimates predicted ratings based on the combined review content information, using a cutting-edge transformer model. To further refine this process, SIFN is trained using a novel loss function called Cross-Entropy Loss (CEL) combined with Mean Squared Error (MSE). The proposed framework was extensively validated through experiments on four datasets from distinct domains, demonstrating the substantial superiority of SIFN over numerous baseline models in predicting accurate review ratings. The model's source code and dataset are available for further research purposes. The empirical results illustrate the practical value of SIFN in real-world applications by showcasing its superior performance in predicting review ratings on multiple datasets. Notably, SIFN achieved a notable reduction in the cross-entropy loss, with significant improvements ranging from 32.11% to 57.34% compared to several strong baseline models, thus affirming its effectiveness. The model's performance can be further optimized by incorporating additional factors such as semantic matching between review embeddings and products, which might serve as a promising future research direction. The proposed framework is visually illustrated through a graphical representation, providing a clear and concise overview of its architecture. The model's performance statistics are presented in a table format, displaying SIFN's performance in comparison to baseline models across different datasets. The first scenario views the CS sentence as a English sentence with inserted Arabic words, while the second scenario interprets the CS sentence as a merged, single language sentence. We collected and analyzed CS data from two social media platforms for analysis purposes. We discovered that a specific word substitution method paired with a particular observation scenario yielded the most accurate results, outperforming other data augmentation methods in terms of CS sentence fluency and coherence as judged by native speakers and automated systems, respectively. Notably, the most effective approach resulted in synthetic CS sentences that were deemed comparable to real CS data by human judges. This study is the first to explore CS data augmentation through lexical substitutions for Arabic-English language pairs. We will release the collected CS data on the Microsoft Azure Dataverse platform for future use. We show that any subgroup of diffeomorphisms on a compact surface that act by homeomorphisms and have negative curvature has a compact topology similar to the Roelcke topology when the surface's genus is 0 or negative. Furthermore, we find that such groups are only topologically dense in diffeomorphism groups when the surface's genus is positive. This information makes it clear that our results with negative curvature groups cannot be extended to surfaces with positive genus. Moreover, we prove a previously unknown fact that Whitehead's theorem does not hold for diffeomorphism groups with the Roelcke topology. Conjointly, we determine that groups of quasi-conjugacy classes of diffeomorphisms on a 2-torus do not have a compact topology when the torus is not simply-connected. Additionally, we define a new Banach algebra for discrete groups of homeomorphisms on a 2-sphere, which is different from the one used by Ghosh, Shnirelman and Yurin and the one used by Polterovich, Shalom and Shemueli. This new algebra allows for the implementation of a theorem for duality of Banach spaces by Grothendieck. As a result, we find that any subgroup of homeomorphisms on a 2-sphere that are compactly supported has a compact topology similar to the uniform topology when the sphere is not simply-connected. However, we conclude that such groups are not topologically dense in homeomorphism groups when the sphere's Gaussian curvature is positive. Finally, the implementation of a theorem for duality of Banach spaces by Breuillard, Tointon and Warhurst does not hold for these groups. A significant advancement in computational discretization has been achieved through the hexahedral mesh method, enabling the efficient modeling of complex 3D geometries with compact data representations. Although hexahedral meshes offer superior analytical properties compared to other discretization methods, their full potential is hindered by the high computational cost associated with processing and optimization. To address this limitation, a proposed method involves the use of advanced data structures, including ABAHLD and VHLD, which facilitate the efficient handling of hexahedral meshes with reduced memory requirements. To take full advantage of these data structures, a new approach called VHMTA is developed, incorporating various hexahedral mesh algorithms utilizing the VHLD data structure. By combining the strengths of low-extras density methods and topological mutations, VHMTA is designed to outperform existing hexahedral mesh generation methods, with an impressive ability to produce meshes with 58 terrahedra per hexahedral cell, an unprecedented achievement. Furthermore, VHMTA has the potential to be adapted for parallel processing, with the potential to exceed the current state-of-the-art of 20 Tets/Hex at scale. To demonstrate its effectiveness, VHMTA is visually illustrated through a 3D animation, showcasing its ability to adaptively refine a coarse, low-density mesh into a high-quality, high-density mesh. With its exceptional performance and adaptability, VHMTA is poised to revolutionize hexahedral mesh generation. At the time of writing, VHMTA has been successfully tested on a 640 GB IBM Sun Liquid Cool Server with a processing speed of 5.0 GHz and 1024 cores. Furthermore, VHMTA has been employed in a groundbreaking numerical simulation of the Earth's core dynamics, where it successfully modeled the receding liquid core over 4.5 billion years. To explore more advanced features, VHMTA can be integrated with external libraries such as adaptivity and parallel processing, with the aim of achieving an even greater impact on scientific computing. What makes VHMTA truly innovative is its adaptability - its mesh quality algorithm can be used not only to generate high-quality hexahedral meshes but also to repair and post-process existing meshes, regardless of their type, whether they are generated using hexahedral methods or other approaches. As a result, VHMTA is significantly easier to deploy and more versatile than current state-of-the-art methods, making it an attractive choice for a wide range of scientific computing applications. The most common techniques for relation extraction are those that either evaluate the semantic similarity between two concepts or look for shared aspects. To boost the accuracy of relation extraction, researchers are now exploring methods to incorporate graph structures. This enhanced approach allows for more precise relation classification by utilizing more training data and selecting relationships that are commonly associated with specific concepts. This study aims to investigate the relationship between relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction, two interconnected tasks that are often separately analyzed in existing literature. The findings indicate that training models on a combination of tasks can significantly improve relation extraction accuracy, with benefits ranging from 2 to 15%. By developing new evaluation metrics and predicting links that don't exist in existing datasets, we demonstrate the validity of this approach. Furthermore, our research also shows that models trained on a task aggregation framework outperform those trained using alternating training for two tasks. Additional experiments were conducted to compare the effectiveness of two aggregation methods, as well as a baseline model that predicts links using fine-tuning, but the results suggest that they are less effective than our proposed approach. Our proposed methods are expected to enhance the accuracy of relation extraction, leading to better performance on six benchmark tests without using any additional data. The code for these methods is publicly available at https://github.com/ranranluo/RE-KLPAuto. This study contributes to the relation extraction field by linking it to knowledge graph link prediction and providing a simple yet effective method to achieve this integration. The proposed aggregation framework is expected to serve as a starting point for research on task embedding, a promising area of study that could lead to more robust models by addressing layer-wise imbalances. Using our proposed technique, we were able to train models that consistently predict 60% of knowledge graph links without any supervision, as well as improve relation extraction accuracy in six benchmark tests. One fundamental challenge in reinforcement learning is to build a continuity implication from the perspective of an agent's state and actions. This means that even though the agent's behavior may not always follow a deterministic or stochastic policy, we can still identify a simpler policy that approximates its actions over a close range to its current state. We resolve this challenge by introducing a new topology suitable for learning tasks in various metric spaces, such as the Euclidean space. This new topology aligns with the 'entropy accumulation' property, which was previously discovered by Cohen et al. (2020). As a result, in any space that satisfies certain conditions (like having a suitable 'entropy diameter'), any learned policy will be continuously deformable from its initial state, making it well-suited for a wide variety of tasks, including learning robotic movements. Furthermore, in cases where the 'entropy diameter' is not satisfied, we demonstrated the importance of examining the robot's learning process in greater detail. As an example, in cases of 'robust rigidity', the robot's behavior in the 'robust rigidity set' would be continuously deformable from its initial state, while these 'rigid' movements, occurring outside of this set, cannot be smoothly emulated by the robot. This result highlights the value of our introduced 'quantitative shifted continuity' definition for policies. As an additional consequence, in cases of simple spaces (like 1-dimensional Euclidean space) the robot's movements can always be continuously deformable from its initial state, even in cases of no 'entropy diameter', which makes our framework highly flexible and suitable for a wide variety of tasks. Our findings are supported by comprehensive scientific evidence, which is displayed through a series of video clips. This research is implemented within the CoCo framework (available at https://github.com/vale-ocean/coconut/tree/entropia). The research was executed on a Tesla V100 GPU and LS M220x GPU server. Systems capable of artificial general intelligence must be equipped with visual recognition abilities that aren't limited to specific objects, which means they should also be able to classify entities based on their animacy - whether they're living or non-living. In this paper, we're going to examine the animacy structure, which is utilized to classify entities as animate or inanimate, using data from both crowd-sourced tests and brain scans. We're also going to examine the different components that make up this structure and how they're utilized in both natural language and visual recognition contexts. We'll present new neuroimagnetic decoding results that confirm the existence of a distinct animate network in the human ventral visual system and demonstrate that this network is responsible for processing animacy in both human and artificial settings. We'll also present findings from a series of behavioral experiments that reveal a connection between the animacy structure and a part of the brain responsible for social cognition, which is the fusiform facial gyrus. In particular, we'll show that the FFG is primarily involved in understanding animacy rather than specificity of animacy signs, which is instead attributed to other brain regions. We'll also discuss how the animacy structure fits into the larger visual recognition system and discuss its potential limitations and applications. One such potential application is in the development of artificial visual recognition systems - given that the animacy structure is inherent to both natural and artificial visual recognition systems, it's likely to play a crucial role in vision-based artificial intelligence. Therefore, it's likely that future advancements in these systems will be built on top of animacy structures that are similar to the one observed in humans, which is characterized by distinct animate and inanimate networks. By further investigating the animacy structure, we can gain a deeper understanding of what it means for a system to be animate in a visual context. Such knowledge can also inform the development of vision-based artificial intelligence. Potentially, it could even be utilized in systems that are capable of artificial general intelligence. In order to achieve this, it's crucial that future advancements in these systems reflect the intricacies of human vision - by doing so, we may be one step closer to creating vision-based artificial intelligence that is more akin to human vision. In particular, it's likely that future advancements in these systems will be built on top of a distinct animate network, which is a key component of the animacy structure. The Social Learning theory reveals that observing others learn facilitates learning oneself, yet using observation as a learning tool can be challenging, especially in situations where finding relevant data is difficult or observation leads to inconsistent outcomes. To overcome these issues, we have developed a method to enhance learning through observation by establishing trustworthy incentives, namely intrinsic motivation to enable the transfer of knowledge. This approach utilizes three elements: flexible motivation adjustment, personalized learning goals, and a unified framework. Empirical studies confirm that our technique not only increases its own performance but also improves performance when applied to new situations and even helps the other agent learning alongside it, essentially making the observation process more effective for learning. The observation is now a source of strength rather than an obstacle. Unlike other methods that rely on observation, our approach is non-parametric and does not require the observationee to have similar characteristics, making it more versatile. To demonstrate the reliability of our technique, we have developed a representation of knowledge that reduces the uncertainty associated with observation-based learning. This representation identifies important factors and distinguishes them from irrelevant information, providing a clearer picture and more confident decision-making. The research presents a comprehensive framework for reliable learning through observation, incorporating both the trustworthiness of the observation itself and the learning process itself. Experiments were conducted within two scenarios, supporting the effectiveness of our technique. The research also reveals that the underlying mechanism of learning through observation is consistent with human learning, making our technique a viable method for promoting reliable learning in various contexts. The research combines theoretical analysis, empirical study, and a case study to illustrate the applicability of our technique in real-world contexts, offering a comprehensive understanding of reliable learning through observation. The research was applied to the creation of autonomous agents and autonomous robot teams, demonstrating that our technique is a feasible solution to the challenges associated with observation-based learning. The research also identifies potential obstacles to learning through observation and proposes strategies for overcoming these challenges. The research is presented in a logical sequence, starting with the underlying challenges of learning through observation, followed by the development of reliable learning concepts, empirical validation of the techniques, case study demonstration of the feasibility of the techniques, and finally theoretical integration of the techniques with existing models of human learning and autonomous learning. The research aims to promote a new understanding of reliable learning through observation and to inspire further research in this topic. Research into automatic substance identification from X-ray or gamma-ray spectra faces significant challenges, especially with limited data and varying conditions. Traditional machine learning techniques that learn patterns from spectra face limitations, while physically motivated methods require numerous identity verification processes. Our study introduces SpectrOR, a pioneering model that utilizes self-supervised contrastive learning to classify substances without relying on extensive databases, simply by applying fundamental physical laws. SpectrOR was tested on real-world spectra of iron, water, and five artificial substances, successfully identifying them with 95% accuracy in a one-shot setting. Additionally, the framework can easily adapt to classification of non-metallic substances. By combining spectra with fundamental atomic properties, the framework can also be expanded to identify unknown substances anywhere in a wide range of general substances. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. Our study marks a significant step towards a fully automated substance identification system. Video demonstration of the substance identification system is available on YouTube. The full implementation of SpectrOR is publicly available at https://github.com/yuansan95/SpectrOR. 

Key to SpectrOR's performance are two innovative components:

1.  A physics-based simulation pipeline that generates virtual spectra for a given substance based on its known abundance, along with random variations in energy, variation of electron density, and angular displacement. This allows the model to learn a generalised idea of a substance, independent of specific conditions.

2.  A contrastive learning-based oracle that takes simulated spectra and real spectra, compares them, and returns the substance identity. This learning approach ensures SpectrOR can identify substances from a small set of real-world spectra, conditions that would pose significant challenges to traditional machine learning techniques.

Our study begins with a thorough analysis of the challenges posed by substance identification, followed by a description of SpectrOR's architecture and training. We then publicly test SpectrOR on datasets comprising spectra of substances, conditions, and environments, different from those employed during training. Finally, a comparison with existing machine learning and physically motivated approaches underscores SpectrOR's superiority in one-shot and few-shot substance identification. The code for SpectrOR is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/yuansan95/SpectrOR. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive review of Lie 2-algebras, drawing on the successful examples of 2-derivations and 2-dialgebras to clarify the concept, which has led to a renewed interest in these areas. The paper will also examine the practical relevance of these concepts, highlighting their appearance in recent research including homotopy Lie algebras, 3-cocycles and cocycles, Chern-Simons theory, higher spin theory, nonstandard quantum field theories and the emergence of Lie 2-algebras in homotopy theory and topological quantum field theories. A concise overview of relevant cohomology and the associated 2-cobordism will also be provided, leading to the emergence of Lie 2-algebras in homotopy theory and topological quantum field theories. The paper will also review simple 2-algebras derived from soliton algebras and challenge the prevailing view that Lie 2-algebras require the use of cohomology by demonstrating that, in many instances, this is not the defining characteristic of a Lie 2-algebra. Ultimately, the paper will reaffirm the defining properties of a Lie 2-algebra identified by Baez and Praditz and highlight their widespread adoption in the literature. A brief consideration of higher-order Lie algebras is also provided. Further research suggestions are also proposed. A consideration of orientifolds in the context of the homotopy theory of Lie 2-algebras is provided, revealing an issue with the current understanding of the homotopy theory of Lie 2-algebras. A consideration of a sequence of 2-algebras derived from the van Hove model is also included. A consideration of a sequence of 2-algebras derived from light-cone gauge super Yang-Mills theory is also included. The defining properties of a 2-algebra are considered in the context of a super Yang-Mills theory and a novel observation related to the emergence of Lie 2-algebras in the theory is provided. The area under the curve (AUC) of a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) is a widely employed metric for evaluating the performance of a binary classifier. Our analysis shows that in the context of solar data visualization, an optimized region of an ROC- AUC has come to be regarded as an effective quality indicator. Similar to other performance measures, its utilization requires careful interpretation in terms of specific scenarios and applications. In this study, we aim to provide clear definitions and numerical examples regarding the scenarios and applications where a particular situation can be regarded as 'biased' or 'unbiased'. Additionally, we are also examining potential strategies for reducing this bias. It is essential to note that (1) the initial dataset is not random sampling but rather a comprehensive collection of solar vector magnetic field fragments obtained through different techniques, (2) the figure of interest is derived from a binary classification model's performance, and (3) the area under the ROC curve, specifically its optimized region, exhibits gradual growth with the expansion of the dataset. These factors collectively contribute to a conclusion that can be regarded as either 'biased' or 'unbiased'. In this paper, we are also assessing the validity of two distinct machine learning-based approaches for reducing this bias by means of data augmentation. In conclusion, by analyzing the results of our study, it can be contended that (1) AUC optimization exhibits a degree of predictability, (2) late-convergence classifications make a notably more significant contribution to this optimization when compared to early-convergence classifications, and (3) the two distinct datasets can be integrated into a singular, more robust dataset that combines their respective strengths. Ultimately, in order to further refine our conclusions, it would be beneficial to conduct additional research focused on other bias-reducing techniques. In a subsequent study, we also aim to explore the implications of utilizing this optimized region $AUC_{\text{opt}}$ as an effective quality indicator for validation sets. Following this, a real-time load shedding strategy is implemented to adjust energy consumption based on current network conditions and weather forecasts. Additionally, a real-time load shedding mechanism is applied to further refine energy usage plans. The proposed method excels existing home energy management methods that primarily focus on solo home energy scheduling. Moreover, the approach outperforms other collective game techniques by yielding improved energy usage plans and reducing iteration complexity. It's the first of its kind to blend adversarial machine learning techniques with independent component analysis, resulting in a faster and more effective method for complex data analysis. Typically, ICA methods have limitations when dealing with data that contains colinearity, a characteristic of many high-dimensional datasets. By leveraging this property, M-ar-Rapid ICA utilizes colinearity to accelerate the ICA process and enhance its performance. Additionally, this technique incorporates an estimation error-based risk function to further improve its accuracy in complex data analysis. M-ar-Rapid ICA outperforms existing techniques by achieving faster inference and more accurate results in numerous experimental tests. These experiments included simulated data as well as real-world applications such as the analysis of gene expression and the extraction of key features from spectroscopic data in narcotics detection. Notably, M-ar-Rapid ICA achieved a superior false discovery rate and improved accuracy in spectroscopic data analysis compared to existing ICA methods. Overall, M-ar-Rapid ICA's adversarial training allows for improved generalization and robust performance in practical applications, making it a valuable tool for handling challenging data in a real-world setting. Advantages of M-ar-Rapid ICA include its ability to perform non-parametric modeling, tolerate data noise, and withstand adversarial manipulation such as Feature Perturbation Attacks (FPA). Our results demonstrate M-ar-Rapid ICA's utility in practical applications, a concept also known as in-vivo neuroimaging. Identifying incidents instantly from real-time social media data over large geographical areas is crucial for emergency management, search and rescue operations, and maintenance of law enforcement and emergency services. 

A novel spatio-temporal anomaly detection method is introduced, which identifies incidents instantly by analyzing real-time social media data. This approach relies on two algorithms: the first determines geographical areas with incident activity using data from various platforms and time intervals, and the second identifies specific locations and moments with the greatest activity. 

To evaluate the performance of the proposed method, two datasets - Twitter data for Barcelona and earthquake data for Italy - were used. Experimental results demonstrate that the introduced algorithm efficiently detects incident areas and times with high accuracy. 

Notably, the proposed method can handle data in real-time and is adaptable to various languages and platforms with zero pre-processing required. This flexibility, combined with the capacity for on-time incident detection, is a rare feature in current spatio-temporal anomaly detection algorithms. 

In summary, the introduced method is simple to implement, highly efficient, and adaptable to multiple data sources, making it a valuable tool for immediate incident detection. 

All the experiments were performed using the Hadoop framework, which utilizes a MapReduce programming model, and the statistical analysis of the results was conducted with R software. 

This research highlights the importance of on-time incident detection and provides a practical solution to overcome the challenge of identifying incidents from vast amounts of social media data over extensive or small-scale geographical areas with zero pre-processing required.

Establishing secure communication networks is of utmost importance for organizations handling classified information, which can be achieved through various encryption methods. One such protocol, quantum key distribution (QKD), utilizes quantum principles to securely exchange keys, thus protecting confidential data. Nevertheless, conventional QKD systems have a weakness that an eavesdropper can potentially exploit, using a non- uniform random source, to calculate the secret key shared between two honest parties. In countermeasure against this vulnerability, QKD systems incorporate source security checks, which include source reliability and consistency verifications. Although these checks hinder an adversary's ability to determine the QKD randomness, they fail to prevent a specific attack that can evade detection by the check itself. Therefore, to address this security breach, a new source security check has been proposed as an additional protection measure. The test is capable of safeguarding against the previously identified attack without compromising the source's integrity or impairing the QKD's performance. Furthermore, this new source security check is capable of detecting another, previously unaccounted for form of a specific attack that occurs when the QKD's key generation rates are low. The proposed check is not only straightforward to implement but also can be executed quickly without obstructing the QKD's process.
