This study presents VACA, a new model for predicting causal effects between a variable and multiple confounding variables, using data that was generated under specific causal conditions. VACA's architecture is based on an extension of the inverse covariance matrix, and it learns to represent both the confounding variables and causal effect dependencies in a way similar to a more common machine learning approach. VACA was tested on a range of different problems, including one where the data was divided into different groups, and it was shown to be able to make predictions about these groups even when it hadn't seen that specific group before. VACA was also compared to other more complex models that can make predictions based on data that wasn't seen during training, and it was shown to be able to make similar predictions using much less data. Additionally, VACA was shown to be able to make predictions about how different individuals would behave under specific hypothetical scenarios, and it was compared to a number of different approaches that can also make these types of predictions. VACA's success suggests that it could be a useful tool for understanding complex systems, and for identifying areas where more data would be helpful for making better predictions. VACA can be found at this github repository. 

Key Words: Causal Inference, Variational Graph Autoencoders, Interventional Queries, Contrafactual Reasoning, Few-shot Experiments, Meta-learning. 

This paper's supplementary information includes more information about the models that were compared to VACA in the experiments, a more detailed description of the different problems that were used in the experiments, and a more detailed description of the different groups that were used in the experiments to test VACA's ability to make predictions about these groups even when it hadn't seen that specific group before.

The most successful films often have a universal appeal due to various factors such as their storyline, direction, or a combination of these elements. While analyzing film profitability can provide insights into the impact of different storylines, it's clear that certain narrative styles have been more profitable than others in the past. Notably, male-led action films have historically generated significant box office revenue, and changes in film characteristics over time reflect this. As the movie industry continues to evolve, so does the success potential of distinct film categories. To explore these trends, we've examined a comprehensive dataset of 684 films from 2010 to 2020, and our findings reveal that certain film types are more likely to be profitable than others. Specifically, our analysis shows that action-comedy films have outperformed other genres in terms of box office income since the late 1990s. We also found that while male-led films continue to earn more than their female-led counterparts, the gender disparity has narrowed in recent years. Interestingly, our data indicates that films produced by a single studio or production company are less successful than those produced independently, and films translated from other languages are more profitable when they maintain their original title. We have also created a novel method to analyze film characteristics, which we've applied to identify patterns and relationships between various film attributes and box office revenue. Our research identifies key factors affecting film profitability, including different storylines, leading actors/actresses, production studios, and distribution methods. While location and time of release are conventional predictors of success, our analysis shows that films promoting social messages are more profitable when they are released during socially conscious times and in locations with high social awareness. Similarly, films showcasing relationships are more profitable when they are released by couples or in locations with high population of couples. Our research implies that successful film traits are not only dependent on the film itself, but also on factors like audience demographics and preferences, which vary by location and time. To this end, we outline present-day film characteristics that are more likely to generate box office revenue, and our research encourages further research in this area by providing access to our dataset and novel method of analysis. We hope our work inspires future research to explore the intersection of film, demographics, and location, ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of the movie industry. In the context of modeling interdependent networks, we propose a new framework that represents each network as a Graphical Labeled Markov Model. This model consists of a directed graph and probabilistic distributions for node and edge states, as well as transition functions that describe how network states evolve over time. Our approach extends the existing GLMark model, which we applied to a network of networks scenario to estimate the probability of failure for interdependent networks following an initial failure. Although primarily focused on large-scale network analysis, our work demonstrates its utility for in-depth fault diagnosis and the determination of the probability of failure for individual nodes. Nevertheless, we recognize the need for a more efficient algorithm to process the vast amounts of data inherent in large-scale networks. To effectively utilize symmetric states in quantum information and quantum field theories, a method to identify them digitally is developed. The proposed approach accurately determines whether a given state is symmetric with high probability using a minimal number of measurements and classical processing, even when the symmetry acts irreducibly on the underlying space and is not simply expressed as a unitary operation. Additionally, this digital identification scheme lays the groundwork for and is incorporated into a novel test of symmetry, which may be utilized in experiments involving quantum systems exhibiting state symmetry. The practical application of this digital scheme is demonstrated using simulations based on a reducible symmetry in systems consisting of up to six qubits. Furthermore, a theoretical framework is established for general states, consisting of multiple components that can be identified digitally, and this is applied to a lab setup aiming to test local CP and anti-CP violations using states of light. It is shown that, in the lab setup, the probabilities of measuring the required outcomes can be expressed as a quadratic function, and the values of these probabilities are maximized when the corresponding components of the state are identified digitally. The proposed digital identification scheme and this theoretical framework can be used for a wide range of quantum information experiments and theoretical calculations involving general states with internal symmetry. The use of simulations is advocated to validate the applicability of identification schemes to practical systems, and the need for careful examination of the underlying physics is emphasized when the symmetry acts irreducibly or lacks a straightforward, local interpretation. The established framework is compatible with various experimental systems, including quantum information experiments involving state preparations, measurements, and classical processing, and the presented calculations are based on a quantum information experiment. The research highlights the importance of leveraging quantum identification schemes in quantum information experiments. The presented theory and simulations demonstrate that digital identification schemes for general states can be employed with high probability, and the research stresses that the applicability of these schemes should not be assumed without examining the underlying physics in depth. The discussion in the thesis is adapted from existing research to address the primary concerns related to the digital identification of symmetric states. A novel approach is proposed for baryon creation, based on a theoretical mechanism called "fractured string" where a baryon forms through the quantized breakdown of a QCD thread of finite thickness that exhibits left-handed rotation. This QCD thread, visualized as a helically twisting filament, has thickness of order of the pion radius, and its breakdown into fundamental strings occurs when it exceeds the scale of the baryon at a point of left-handed rotation. Baryon creation is thereby associated with the localization of a color charge on one of the breaking strings, resulting in three fundamental strings with a color charge of one and three, respectively. This theoretical mechanism proposes that baryons embody color sources separated by distant quarks, in contrast to the traditional concept. Additionally, we conclude that the breaking of QCD threads through their internal helicity is naturally conducive to the creation of baryons, and the resulting process could contribute to understanding baryon mass distribution as well as their strong interaction patterns. Moreover, this theoretical mechanism may offer an explanation for observed yield ratios of baryons over mesons in high-energy laboratory collisions. Yield ratios of baryons over mesons are found to be close to 1 in collisions at very high energies, and this theoretical mechanism provides an explanation for this phenomenon. Yield ratios are determined using elementary baryon creation dynamics in a string framework, and in addition to confirming theoretical predictions, it is found that Y meson yields in laboratory collisions are predominantly a result of two-string dynamics, and consequently, predictions for meson yields in collisions at higher energies are not significantly affected by three-string dynamics. However, it is expected that three-string dynamics will start to significantly affect yields at much higher energies than currently observed. Furthermore, predictions for yield ratios of baryons over mesons are found to be constant with respect to energy at an average value of approximately 0.75, and the predicted yield ratios agree with yield ratios observed in laboratory collisions at energies of 8.16 and 13 GeV. In addition to agreeing with yield ratio observations in laboratory collisions at various energies, our theoretical predictions provide insight into baryon creation mechanisms as well as distribution patterns at a microscopic level. Ultimately, it is found that baryon creation through QCD thread breakdown is a ubiquitous baryon creation mechanism, and it is proposed that this theoretical concept be referred to as the fractured string model of baryon creation. Our study examines how gravitational waves generated during inflation are embedded 
in the variance of Pulsar Timing Array dishes to identify indirect signs of 
electromagnetic field presence in the early universe.  Since electromagnetic 
forces prevail over gravitational waves during inflation, the latter are enveloped 
by electromagnetic waves.  We propose that these waves, caused by quantum fluctuations 
in electromagnetic fields, produce GWT signals, which, in turn, are detected as a 
variable Pulsar Timing Array frequency modulation.  We calculated the variance 
of this modulation for PSR J1534$-$52, PSR J1903+32, and PSR B1855+24 and found it to 
be within the current research limits.  We further found that this modulation's frequency 
range, 1$\times$10$^{-19}$ to 2$\times$10$^{-18}$ Hz, is consistent with the Pulsar 
Timing Array frequency band, which corresponds to the primordial electromagnetic 
fields' scale of 10$^{-3}$ to 10$^{-1}$ Mpc.  We also found that this phenomenon's 
detectability largely depends on the Pulsar Timing Array dishes' area, with the J1534$-$52 
Pulsar having a 100 m diameter, which is adequate for detecting the gravitational wave 
frequency modulation.  We also considered a model in which the initial electromagnetic 
field fluctuations, caused by quantum gravity effects, resulted in the generation of 
primordial gravitational waves, which, in turn, produced a variable modulation frequency 
in the Pulsar Timing Array dishes to yield null results, as no modulation frequency 
was observed within the Pulsar J1534$-$52 variance.  We further found that this model's 
predictive powers, which correspond to the primordial gravitational waves' amplitude 
and frequency, are inconsistent with the Pulsar J1534-$52 variance results, as well as 
the Pulsar B1855+24 results.  We also found that these powers, which correspond to 
the gravitational wave amplitude and frequency, are within the Pulsar J1903+32

frequency corresponds to 2$\times$10$^{-19}$ Hz.  We also found that the Pulsar J1903+32 
recoverable signal could be readily detected with the 100 m diameter Pulsar J1534

In the context of federated learning, where data remains on users' devices, the aggregation of models is possible without data collection by a central entity, making the process more viable due to data retention concerns and the need for user confidentiality. Despite these benefits, the equilibrium achieved through FL is often unjust, as heterogeneous data causes the collective model to favor performance on the data held by the majority of users, potentially leading to poor results for users with unique data sets. Furthermore, the possibility of revealing an individual's identity from their updated model poses a significant risk, as this model is shared with others during the FL process. We introduce the first formulation of differential privacy in the FL setting and propose a method that preserves privacy while promoting equity. We then provide a numerical demonstration of the trade-off between equity and privacy, highlighting potential consequences that are counterintuitive. Our study ultimately shows that achieving both equity and privacy using FL is challenging and may require a closer look at the data aggregation method. We also begin exploring alternative techniques for achieving equity in the FL setting. The study was published in the Proceedings of the 2022 Conference of the Council for Professional Informatics (2022.CPI) under the title \emph{Equity Without Privacy: A Case Study in Federated Learning} and is available at \url{https://arxiv.org/pdf/2202.00987.pdf}. We introduce an unsupervised learning approach to optimize a wireless powered network in non-line-of-sight scenarios disrupted by interference. A key challenge arises from the absence of interference maps. We propose the creation of approximate maps through observations of reflected signals by an IRS. A deep learning-based algorithm combines global optimization and local exploration to optimize IRS phase shifts and the transmitter's energy allocation, while its simplified form reduces computational complexity. We confirm that our unsupervised learning-based solution can yield comparable performance to a informed method, while local exploration enables generalizability to previously unencountered scenarios. This study proposes a method for producing high-quality annotations through
involved image processing, which can facilitate object detection within various
domains without relying on expert supervision. A unique data structure, 'open
lexicons', lists objects within a given domain to aid in this process. Since
object detection frameworks rely on image coordinates for an accurate match,
we suggest 'pseudo-annotations' to bridge the gap between open lexicons and
object detection models. These pseudo-annotations are learned through a unique
annotation of image data with lexical information. The results show that pseudo-
annotations enhance object detection performance when compared to traditional
supervised methods. Notably, our approach also improves state-of-the-art results in
specific domains with limited resources, namely zero-shot handwriting and drug
package detection. The associated code and dataset will be publicly available.  A
related manuscript has been previously published in the workshops of the 2022 IJCAI and NeurIPS conferences.

Convolutional neural networks achieve superior performance by incorporating the inherent structure of images, but the role of weight pruning in CNNs remains distinct from that in traditional neural networks.  While a notable reduction in parameters can be realized in CNNs with minimal loss in accuracy, prior studies indicate that the optimal pruning technique for CNNs is highly dependent on the specific architecture, making it a uniquely challenging issue to resolve.  We discovered that the primary factor inhibiting weight pruning in CNNs is the overly broad distribution of weights within each filter, rather than the spatially localized covariance of convolutional layers.  By utilizing trimming, an adaptive regularization technique, we are able to enhance the convexity of the loss surface and achieve more targeted weight reduction, along with improved generalization after pruning.  Furthermore, our findings suggest that the optimal pruning methodology for fully-connected layers is distinct from that of convolutional layers, and that trimming offers a suitable solution to achieve compelling results from state-of-the-art models.  Ultimately, our experiments demonstrate that with trimming, it is possible to identify and eliminate unnecessary parameters in world-leading models such as VGG-BN and ResNet, yielding substantial savings in parameters while minimizing a manageable loss in inference accuracy.  We observed that the trimmed model often outperforms the sparse model consisting only of the essential 'lottery ticket' parameters, indicating that the key to success lies in identifying and targeting unnecessary parameters rather than solely focusing on the essential ones.  We have released the code for trimming to facilitate its application in addressing the challenging issue of weight pruning in convolutional neural networks.  What is more, our findings emphasize the significance of further investigating the interplay between pruning and the spatial structure of data, as well as evaluating the influence of trimming on the dynamics of gradient vanishing/flow using numerical tools and analytical methods, such as neural tangent kernels.  Ultimately, our study points to a promising research direction, namely, exploring trimming-friendly architectures that are inherently more amenable to weight pruning, potentially reducing the computational expense associated with trimming and enabling its seamless integration with other methods.  In doing so, we have identified an intriguing research hypothesis, namely, that networks possessing quasi-local covariance properties can be more easily trimmed to achieve sparse models with minimal loss in accuracy, in line with our findings on the target distribution of trimmed weights having a notably more localized character compared to the prior distribution.  What is more, our research hypothesis is closely related to a novel architectural research direction, namely that networks with a large kernel size are more amenable to weight pruning

This technical report presents our technical solutions to three challenges in the NeurIPS 2022 Competition on Visual Domain Adaptation: universal domain adaptation, universal multi-way adaptation, and universal multi-domain adaptation. Our approaches leverage two techniques - R1 max-pooling for eliminating batch norms and an exponential moving average for maintaining domain adaptation stability. Notably, we obtained first-place rankings in the universal domain adaptation and universal multi-domain adaptation tasks, and a second-place ranking in the universal multi-way adaptation task. Our findings and implemented code are available on GitHub at https://github.com/Phryce/ADA. 

Key
---

In this report, we outline our strategy for solving each of the three domain adaptation challenges in the NeurIPS 2022 Competition.

Challenge 1: Universal Domain Adaptation
We discovered that the widely-used ResNet architecture suffers from a flaw known as batch normalization paralysis. Our research indicates that the R1 max-pooling method, proposed by J. S. Weber (2021), can effectively remedy this issue. For training, we employed an exponential moving average with a significant gamma value, as suggested by S. Korneli (2020). Notably, our approach combined with a deeply-mixed hard example mining technique resulted in the highest validation accuracy across all tested datasets.

Challenge 2: Universal Multi-way Adaptation
Given that the multi-way adaptation is a subset of universal domain adaptation, we primarily focused on optimizing our universal adaptation approach to achieve the best results for each source domain. Our approach yielded a second-place ranking in the universal multi-way adaptation challenge.

Challenge 3: Universal Multi-domain Adaptation
We observed that the "multi-domain" term is often used ambiguously to describe both universal multi-way adaptation and generalizable training. In this challenge, we focused on the latter, where our universal multi-way adaptation approach was further refined by incorporating a simple weight averaging method for enhancing training robustness across multiple adaptation tasks. Our results earned a first-place ranking in the universal multi-domain adaptation challenge.

In conclusion, our report provides an in-depth analysis of our strategy for solving the three domain adaptation challenges in the NeurIPS 2022 Competition, as supported by the accompanying code available on GitHub at https://github.com/Phryce/ADA.

In this research, a universal digital-analog hybrid approach is presented for simulating complex many-particle systems on a quantum computer. By combining a classical pattern generator with a linear amplifier and a network of single microwave qubits, this method enables the creation of interacting many-particle states. Our demonstration, which successfully emulated a Fermionic-Hubbard model using two Fermionic qubits, resulted in the simulation's wavefunction and quasiparticle spectrum aligning closely with the expected outcomes. Furthermore, precise knowledge of the superconducting qubits was not necessary for the simulation. Our research showcases the potential of hybrid quantum computing methods in efficiently modeling intricate physical systems. This technology may lead to the development of novel and innovative materials with unique properties, potentially resulting from digital-analog quantum simulations. An essential aspect of this method's viability for large-scale simulations is the development of sophisticated yet low-cost analog devices, with potential for the methods to be adapted and improved with the advancement in quantum error correction protocols. An exhaustive technical description of the emulated circuit is provided in an accompanying study. Our approach leverages a specific physical mechanism and, therefore, its applicability might be limited to certain areas within quantum physics research. An alternative method, described in 'Digital-analog simulation of bosonic systems and discovery of a light bulb-like excitation in a circuit' article, achieves a trade-off between cost, knowledge requirement, and accuracy, though at the expense of a more complicated circuit. Both approaches share a common goal of efficiently modeling complex many-body systems on a quantum computer.

Recent decades have seen the prevalence of traditional in-office working arrangements gradually shift towards flexible remote working setups. Despite Scrum adoption increasing among software teams in recent years, the impact of remote working on their project outcomes remains unclear. This research aims to explore the relationship between remote work and Scrum project success using a comprehensive dataset of 1,105 projects. Our initial analysis revealed a significant project success loss associated with remote work across the board. Furthermore, we identified and sequentially tested potential mediators and moderators of this effect, finding that remote working's negative impact on project success could be explained by decreased team morale and increased work hours but not by improved communication between team members. Our findings also suggest that well-managed communications can mitigate the negative effects of remote work on project success in Scrum projects. They provide valuable insights for organizations contemplating a transition to remote working arrangements. They may also shed light on how to implement such changes in a way that maximizes project success. They can even guide and inform the development of theories regarding remote working's effects. Ultimately, our project offers a potential research path to explore the complex interplay between remote working and software project management. Our team aimed to explore the relationship between remote work and project success within these projects. Our analysis was based on a unique dataset that combined project success and working arrangement information with team-related variables extracted from comprehensive datasets and objectively measured variables like team size and technology usage. Our findings were consistent across different models that measured project success in different ways. We identified and tested specific variables that could explain the relationship between remote work and project success. Our analysis revealed that team morale and not team size influenced project success. Our analysis also showed that work hours, not working hours per week, impacted project success. Our analysis of communications data, including daily working hours, call duration, team size, and used communication tools, allowed us to explain the effect of remote work on project success. We found potential team morale and increased work hours to be potential solutions to mitigate the negative impact of remote work on project success. The conventional response involves recalculating optimal routes for each update, but this protracted process can cause delays due to the rising demand for more buses. A proposed solution involves dividing the updating process into smaller tasks and assigning them to a central server for efficient management, allowing for the simultaneous updating of multiple systems. By sharing processing power, the central server can efficiently prioritize tasks - updating one company's schedules as quickly as possible while still providing accurate results. A major advantage of this approach is the potential for real-time collaboration, enabling the rapid updating of multiple schedules while minimizing the risk of errors. The suggested solution involves the creation of a distributed system - a central server and multiple companies sharing a database - allowing for the simultaneous updating of multiple bus company schedules. By utilizing established technologies - a MySQL database and Java servers - the central server can prioritize tasks from multiple companies, ensuring that each update is carried out as quickly and with as little disruption as possible. The suggested solution was tested using simulated company data, demonstrating that the central server can prioritize tasks effectively and update schedules efficiently. The solution was also evaluated based on its distributed transaction characteristics, concluding that the use of shared processing has a limited impact on system performance. The solution's effectiveness was further assessed by simulating real-time updates to multiple company schedules over a period of one year, revealing that the central server can update multiple company schedules efficiently while minimizing the risk of errors. This paper focuses on the mechanical aspects of a single-legged hopping robot's movement, exploring how its force application affects the impact dynamics when it steps down on a deformable surface. To better understand these impacts, we simulated various hopping scenarios using a validated force-based model through extensive experimental verification. Beyond analyzing existing behaviors, we used a non-linear optimization technique to develop three strategies for enhancing the robot's performance by adjusting its actuator effort at the moment of foot placement. Our simulations demonstrate the potential for significant improvements in the robot's stability and efficiency through these optimized control approaches. Furthermore, we identified the limits within which the robot can successfully deploy the enhanced strategies without compromising its stability. Ultimately, this research aims to provide a comprehensive framework for designing more robust and efficient single-legged hopping robots. 

Keywords: Hopping robots, soft terrain, optimization, walking algorithms, legged locomotion, multi-body dynamics, force-based models, nonlinear programming.

One approach, which involves locating the phase shift where the localized phase transitions to a delocalized phase, has yielded a phase diagram that contrasts with the typical volume law expected in non-localized systems. Notably, the critical region exhibits a non-unique self-similar pattern, characterized by a fractal dimension greater than one, indicating that different localized eigenstates display a diverse and highly dispersed set of local correlations. Studying these critical behaviors and the metric properties of these eigenstates with Lévy distibutions enables researchers to develop techniques for detecting localization and delocalization and to gain insight into the nature of criticality. Furthermore, the concept of multifractality is found to not only mark criticality but also occur across the entire phase shift where localized and delocalized phases coexist, potentially obliterating the idea of distinct phases in the system. As a result, Lévy distribution is found to be an essential component in developing techniques for detecting phase shifts in many-body localized systems. Furthermore, the concept of multifractality is found to not only mark criticality but also occur across entire phase shifts in the system where localized and delocalization coexist, potentially obliterating the idea of distinct phases in the system. Consequently, the concept of multifractality is found to be fundamental in determining phase shifts in many-body localized systems. Lastly, the systematic application of concepts in fractal geometry and the metric properties of eigenstates may offer new avenues for distinguishing localized, critical, and delocalized phases in the system. Nearly spherical domains are a specific type of manifold where the boundary is minimal and has a constant mean curvature close to that of a sphere.  Using a novel method that combines geometric techniques and a spectral shift argument, we calculate the asymptotic behavior of these eigenvalues as the norm of the nearly spherical condition converges to zero.  Additionally, we determine the order of the first non-zero Steklov eigenvalue for three-dimensional nearly spherical domains.  Our findings also apply to surfaces with constant curvature.  Finally, for three-dimensional volumes that are nearly spherical, we calculate the asymptotic behavior of both Neumann and Dirichlet eigenvalues and demonstrate their similarity in proportionality, consistent with the behavior of the spherical case.  Notably, for nearly spherical volumes, the orders of the Neumann and Dirichlet eigenvalues differ significantly, exhibiting distinct powers of the convergence norm.  Our study includes various counterexamples to verify the accuracy of the calculated asymptotic behaviors for Steklov eigenvalues.  These counterexamples specifically contradict multiple conjectures related to the spectral behavior of nearly spherical domains.  They also disrupt a proposed inequality between Neumann and Dirichlet eigenvalues, showing that the conjecture can only be achieved asymptotically.  Our research establishes that the conjecture holds in the case of spherical boundaries but fails for boundaryless three-dimensional manifolds with constant negative curvature.  Ultimately, for a vast set of nearly spherical domains, the asymptotic behavior of the lower Neumann eigenvalues follows a distinct specification, and we have a certain uncertainty regarding the lower Dirichlet eigenvalues.  To resolve this uncertainty, we present multiple examples to demonstrate that the lower Dirnev eigenvalues can occur at a distinct rate of convergence, depending on whether the conjugacy spectrum is simple or has a repeated value.  These examples demonstrate a significant aspect: for domains with a simple conjugacy spectrum, the rate of convergence is faster than what is predicted through principal symbol estimates.  Our research addresses a related open problem by achieving the principal result in the case of spherical boundaries.  To achieve this result, we combine a spectral shift argument with distinct approaches: first, the case of boundaryless three-dimensional manifolds with constant positive scalar curvature, and second, the case of three-dimensional nearly spherical domains.  Our research also includes a relevant example to demonstrate a specified uncertainty regarding the asymptotic behavior of the lower Dirnev eigenvalues. The development of a rigorous semantics is fundamental, as it enables the clarification of a concept and identifies potential issues. This paper delves into the semantics of temporal planning, examining and proving the properties of temporal constraints, before introducing a formal validation within a first-order logic framework. By providing a comprehensive semantics, we can ensure that planning problems are properly defined, and the failure of a plan due to incorrect input can be distinguished from failure due to insufficient solution strategies. Additionally, our findings indicate that the semantics of classical planning, based on structures, is inherently linked to the semantics of temporal planning, which utilizes models. This connection justifies the adoption of the classical planning semantics for temporal planning, and we recommend its use as the default approach. However, for precision, we propose utilizing the term 'temporal solution' to denote a plan that resolves the input problem, and to define failure as the absence of a temporal solution. This paper also provides a formal definition of well-definedness for transition planning problems, and demonstrates that if such a problem is well-defined, every input instance will have either a temporal solution or be marked as unsolvable. These findings contribute to the progression of theoretical foundations in planning. Further research could focus on embedding the defined semantics into a widely used planning framework, and further examining the notion of unsolvable instances. As a result of our study, we can now confirm that the planning tool, Tesson, adheres to the defined semantics. This tool's compliance enables the evaluation and assessment of the performance capabilities, particularly the scalability, of temporal planning algorithms, which has been a long-standing challenge. By confirming Tesson's adherence to the defined semantics, we facilitate the collection and presentation of a benchmark suite for temporal planning, which can aid in the evaluation and comparison of future planning algorithms. A benchmark suite would yield valuable insights into the potential for future design and improvement. This paper is set to be presented at the ICAPS 2022 conference. In the long term, we intend to expand the defined semantics to advanced planning techniques, which rely on heuristic methods and dynamic planning, and to integrate the established benchmark suite into the Planning Competition system, the de facto standard for evaluating and comparing planning approaches. This integration would enable the assessment and analysis of the defined semantics, as well as the performance capabilities of advanced planning algorithms. Although the defined semantics of temporal planning lacks a current benchmark suite, we are now in a position to create and contribute one. In concept maps, concepts serve as the fundamental units of information, with each having its own definition. However, definitions are typically not provided; instead, relevant text data containing the desired concept is given along with a list of definitions, and a reader must search for the applicable definition. To replicate this concept in the real world, this research paper proposes Search Term Based Concept Positioning, where a device utilizes voice as the input, and renders definitions visually based on the speaker's intended meaning. To accomplish this, the paper introduces a new model called STRICT, which combines two existing models for speech-to-text analysis and concept classification, and includes a new dataset with corresponding data. The paper also explores several positioning techniques and a user interface, ultimately demonstrating that speech is an effective and natural interface for accessing information. The proposed system, which is part of a larger platform, was evaluated through two studies that assessed its accuracy and usability. Findings revealed that, although the system's concept recognition performance could still be improved, it received positive reviews from users regarding its usability. Building on this technology, the project envisions a web application called WebSpeak, which allows users to search for information by speaking, rather than typing. Although WebSpeak is still in its early stages of development, it has the potential to significantly enhance the browsing experience for individuals who struggle with typing due to various impairments. The WebSpeak source code, including the STRICT model and study results, has been publicly released for further development. In particular, areas for potential improvement were identified as the domain adaptation for speech recognition and incorporating more relevant concepts during training. The project's next goals involve improving the system's performance in these areas through techniques such as data augmentation, and integrating WebSpeak with other related projects, which prioritize natural human-device interaction. Ultimately, the project's long-term ambition is to establish a comprehensive, user-friendly platform that enables natural interaction between devices and humans, and empowers users to freely express themselves. Colloidally derived gels have garnered attention for their extended shelf life and ease of transportation. Yet, they lack flexibility in terms of flow properties, mechanical resilience, and suitability for various applications. To address these limitations, researchers have developed a novel concept - rheo-acoustic gels - incorporating acoustic vibrations during processing. Ultrasonic energy enhances gel formation, adjusts colloid particle distribution, and improves gel structure, ultimately allowing for customization of gel rheological properties. Experiments examining carbopol gel formation with vibrated and static colloid suspensions revealed a reduction in minimum vibration energy required to trigger gelation in the vibrated suspension as vibration frequency increased. Moreover, the viscoelastic properties and yield stress of the gel exceeded those of the static suspension, and vibrated suspensions exhibited improved shear thinning behavior and reduced residual strain. The impact of vibration intensity and duration on gel properties was also explored, revealing optimal gel characteristics at specific vibration parameters. The introduction of acoustic vibrations during processing enables the production of advanced gels with improved mechanical strength, flexibility, and efficiency, opening up new possibilities in food, personal care, and pharmaceutical applications. The possibility of controlling gel structure and properties to create complex microstructures has also emerged, potentially allowing for the creation of multi-functional materials. The main obstacles to implementing this technology are the limitations on its flow characteristics, mechanical resilience, and long-term stability. Nonetheless, researchers have successfully extended the shelf life and improved the flow properties of the gel, and future studies will focus on developing tools to assess and analyze gel flow characteristics. The concept of rheo-acoustic gels has the potential to significantly expand the spectrum of available gels and create new opportunities in various industries. The long-term stability of the gel remains a challenge, but it can be improved by optimizing colloid and gel composition, and by monitoring gel properties over time to identify factors that affect long-term stability. Researchers have found that vibrated gels exhibit improved rheological properties but limited improvement in long-term stability. Therefore, future studies should focus on developing methods to enhance both the short-term and long-term characteristics of the gel. This paper presents a concise overview of the conjecture, focusing on key research aspects and expressing my own prediction: despite the undetermined status of the conjecture after nearly a century, I believe it will be proven in the near future. The efficiency of neural network-based object detection methods for real-time applications heavily relies on proposal generation. Typically, neural networks are designed to minimize mean average precision to achieve high accuracy, although this goal is conflicting since precision requires more proposals, which inversely consumes more memory and increases processing time. To address this, a new method, called Stable Pairing, has been proposed for the Faster R-CNN detection model, aiming to optimize proposal generation to achieve a balance between accuracy and efficiency. This approach involves a novel loss function that adapts to the FPN anchor biases, utilizing the relative ranking of the score of a regressed point to that of a fixed reference point, which significantly reduces the variance of the proposal distribution while maintaining key information. As a result, the method yields a notable 8-12% decrease in FPN PPA without compromising mean average precision, also shrinking inference time by a substantial 11-18.5% in the case of Faster R-CNN with FPN. Furthermore, the approach outperforms FPN PPA in the PADA-FRCNN model, also reducing inference time by a substantial 13-20.5%. Additionally, the approach enhances the accuracy of the YOLOv5 model, lowering mean AP by a notable 3.5-5.5% with only a minimal 0.1-0..15% increase in model size, also reducing inference time by a substantial 8-17% when applied to the MS-COCO benchmark. This method is freely accessible at https://github.com/TrueBack/Stable-Pairing. The code for the YOLOv5 model is at https://github.com/TrueBack/YOLOv5-SP. Current evaluation metrics for summarization tasks have their limitations. Existing guidelines do not thoroughly consider the varied goals of summarization, leading to summaries that may not accurately reflect the intended outcome and are not adequately measured. Due to the restrictive nature of previous metrics, they struggle to evaluate summaries effectively, especially those that deviate from the conventional conservative style. Furthermore, since these metrics rely solely on surface-level text analysis, they ignore the nuances of summarization such as discarding irrelevant information and incorporating knowledge. Our proposed solution is SummScore, a comprehensive evaluation metric that assesses a summary's quality by evaluating how closely it aligns with its corresponding origin text. To achieve this, SummScore leverages the assistance of a powerful transformer-based language model and operates through two distinct phases. During the initial phase, it generates a set of summary descriptions, followed by a second phase where it estimates the quality of each description. To ensure the effectiveness of our metric, we have compiled a substantial dataset comprising $38$ million training examples, $2$ million test examples, and substantially expanded the original CoSum corpus for our research. By evaluating SummScore against leading previous metrics using both human assessments and automated testing on multiple datasets, it has consistently demonstrated superior performance, demonstrating a significant improvement of up to $3.21$ and an average increase of $1.45$ in evaluation accuracy. Furthermore, SummScore has been found to be robust in various scenarios, capable of handling summaries that vastly diverge from the original text and even those written in different styles. Additionally, it shows minimal bias towards specific types of summarization that often employ a conservative tone. Our research suggests that SummScore offers a more versatile and versatile evaluation method for the field of summarization. It is noteworthy that SummScore excels particularly when compared to alternative metrics such as BERTScore and COMET, indicating its potential as a valuable tool in the community. Given its promising performance across multiple datasets, it has been made publicly available for the research community at https://github.com/asharman/SummScore. While our research has yielded significant findings, it also identifies areas for further investigation and potential limitations of the method. Notably, it appears that SummScore exhibits slight bias towards summaries containing knowledge, warranting future exploration of this phenomenon. The conventional approach to 3D detection, primarily rooted in LiDAR and video fusion, starts with individual feature extractions that are then merged through specialized matching modules, yet this solution is riddled with problems including inconsistent features, uncertainty fluctuations, and poor localizations. To overcome these limitations, we're evolving this approach by using an adaptable fusion framework that equates features across modalities, thereby streamlining the extractions and allowing direct concatenation and fusion of multi-modal data. By simplifying the framework, we're also enhancing our model's capacity for explicit semantic reasoning between the LiDAR and camera, resulting in a more robust and accurate 3D detection system. According to our experiments on the KITTI dataset, our novel fusion framework not only outperforms current state-of-the-art models but also offers more transparent and intuitive 3D detection outcomes. Nonetheless, using multivariate kernel estimators may compromise results by requiring intricate computations and large sample sizes. Conversely, nonparametric approaches like the shortest length minimax estimator demonstrate robust performance and are simpler to compute, especially when the true conditional expectation function is unknown. Interestingly, these estimators can also be useful in a universal setting where the true conditional expectation function remains unknown. Ultimately, this trend persists when incorporating additional characteristics such as missing data and multivariate random variables, and can be further analyzed using properties and principles of empirical distribution functions. Moreover, these concepts can also be applied to estimate conditional quantile functions and develop a novel shortest length minimax estimator for a given quantile. The efficacy of these ideas has been substantiated through concrete examples and simulations that highlight their practical value, and preclude the need for cumbersome parametric assumptions. As an example of this approach, we examine a real-world dataset from the CD4 Time series experiment to illustrate the effectiveness of these estimators in a applied setting. The underlying methodology employs techniques similar to those described above and has been made available as the cd4test R package for public use. The cd4test package provides a versatile and flexible set of tools for working with empirical distribution functions and shortest length minimax estimators, and has been designed with the goal of producing simple, robust, and efficient results. The resulting output was plotted and provided as an example of how these tools have been implemented in the cd4test package. The framework is designed with modularity in mind, allowing for an in-depth investigation of complex trade-offs between observation frequency, precision, and potential infection risks. With the framework's versatility, it can easily be applied to various types of observations, data distribution methods, and algorithms for state estimation. The proposed framework also yields new insights into the challenges of accurate state estimation, particularly when using infrequent or noisy data that complicates the correction of state estimates. The results illustrate the importance of precise state estimation, even with limited observation frequencies and potential infection risks. However, increasing observation frequencies is shown to be more crucial for enhanced estimation accuracy. Nonetheless, this approach is ultimately hindered by a critical threshold beyond which further observation yields diminishing returns due to inevitable algorithmic noise. The proposed framework is an essential tool for developing and assessing epidemic observation models and their associated algorithms, empowering researchers to design more effective observation strategies for epidemiological applications. A revolutionary machine learning technique allows models to train on edge devices and learn from shared data without moving it, but a major challenge lies in managing resource limitations on these devices. Traditional methods that prioritize minimizing training time aren't sufficient because real-world systems also need to consider energy consumption and reallocation of resources when training. Online federated learning systems typically operate with limited resource allocations and can be interrupted at any time, making it essential to find an asynchronous solution that can adapt to changing resource availability while still minimizing total model training time. We introduce a new nonlinear regression asynchronous federated training algorithm that can work without prior knowledge of resource limitations or model requirements, maintaining fairness by equally considering all participating clients and allocating resources based on model complexity and client delays instead of direct optimization. Our method demonstrates greater efficiency compared to the synchronous approach and a state-of-the-art optimization technique in various real-world systems including Android smartphones, Android Tablets, and Raspberry Pi. Overall, our research confirms that asynchronous federated learning can lead to faster training times while being more energy-efficient and suitable for non-parallelizable tasks. Our method achieves a significant performance increase by up to 43% and matches the convergence performance of the synchronous approach along with a significant reduction in energy consumption by up to 85% with an average delay of only 0.2 seconds. Our code is available at https://github.com/baasvanderwolf/AFAL.

Lastly, the utilization of the singular integral transform method has facilitated the development of an exact closed-form solution to a special case of a nonlinear Schrodinger equation, showcasing the tetration function's role in such systems. In recent times, modeling network representations has received significant attention, particularly with regards to network prediction. The existing approaches, such as Simple Triplets and Deep Tucker, are designed specifically for dense networks. However, networks such as Twitter and Facebook, being vast and sparse, necessitate the development of a new method. To address this concern, we propose Sparsely Structured Network Embedding (SSNE), a novel framework for creating node representations in sparse networks. The SSNE framework comprises two primary modules - a node attention module and a linker module. The former involves the use of a node-specific attention mechanism to derive representations, while the linker module leverages a shallow neural network, such as a logistic regression, to achieve these representations. We compare the performance of SSNE with STA, DT, NH, and LOCAL. SSNE achieves remarkable results, surpassing STA, DT, and NH in accuracy for predicting 2-hop friends and phone contacts, while also outperforming LOCAL on various prediction tasks by making more efficient use of the network. Additionally, SSNE exhibits scalability by only processing a node's nearest neighbor. We also observe that applying a node filter based on the number of shared edges can further reduce SSNE's computational complexity. The experiments further indicate that SSNE's performance shows consistency across real-world sparse social networks. We conclude that SSNE has the potential to derive more accurate node representations in sparse networks. The implementation of SSNE can be found at https://github.com/kevlar/SSNE. We have also made available the derived node representations for the respective networks at https://github.com/kevlar/SSNE-data. The research further highlights that applying a node filter based on the number of shared edges can further reduce SSNE's computational complexity. The SSNE approach thus offers a valuable framework for creating node representations in sparse networks and has the potential to make a significant contribution in this area of research. The research further highlights that modeling network representations, such as those in the SSNE framework, are beneficial across various prediction tasks. The research thus offers a valuable framework for creating node representations in sparse networks and at the same time showcases its practical implications on real-world social networks. The research further offers insights into deriving node representations in sparse networks and proposes a novel framework, SSNE, as a potential alternative to existing methods like STA, DT, and NH. The developed technology allows for a large 1 cm by 1 cm vapor area at a depth of 500 micrometers with minimal depth variations of around 10 micrometers. The produced rubidium vapor has an adjustable density, achieved through regulated oven temperature or gas valve control, that ranges from $10^{10}$ to $10^{13}$ cm$^{-3}$. The integrated structure of our technology supports advanced laser interferometry, such as broadband coherence enhancement and multi-dimensional laser cooling demonstrating cooling to 3E4 kHz bandwidth with 90% purity, that can further lead to reaching the ground state with narrow linewidths. The produced rubidium vapor with long-range interactions could support studies in quantum simulation, additional dimensions, and new physics. The presented technology is also applicable to other alkali metals and can be expanded to wider features or more complex designs. The approach is also compatible with other etching methods such as wet etching and ultra-fast micro-fabrication techniques like LIGA and UML. Wildfires pose a significant threat to global ecosystems and are critical to monitoring and analysis in various fields such as astronomy and meteorology for environmental monitoring. 
Remote sensing via the visible spectrum offers vital information on spatial distribution and speed of wildfires, whereas the thermal spectrum provides crucial insights into fire dynamics, efficiency, and temperature, which are essential factors in determining fire severity and overall risk. 

Currently available fusion techniques for wildfire detection typically rely on traditional in-spection or outdated algorithms. 
Our research introduces a groundbreaking, deep learning-driven infrared-visible fusion technique that surpasses current standards by leveraging the strengths of each spectrum while minimizing their weaknesses. 

Initially, a new metric, Fire Quality Metrics (FQM), is developed to evaluate the performance of generated thermal images that closely resemble those captured by cameras. 
Following this, a new generator, FIRe-GAN, is designed to perform infrared-visible fusion, leveraging the strengths of each spectrum while minimizing their weaknesses. 
Additionally, this approach aims to increase the scalability of the training process, allowing it to be expanded to high-resolution images that are crucial for determining fire severity.

Early detection and treatment of depression is crucial to prevent severe repercussions, making the development of timely detection methods essential.  While mental health professionals rely heavily on client confessions, researchers now employ machine learning to automatically identify depressive tendencies from vast amounts of digital data.  Focusing on social media posts as a primary source, this study collects and analyzes 21,772 posts from 2,211 users spanning 313 days to create an extensive training dataset.  By comparing four diverse feature extraction methods for text classification, this study evaluates the effectiveness of different machine learning algorithms on the resulting dataset, ultimately providing empirical evidence that supports the automatic detection of depression from social media posts.  Moreover, this study proposes a novel protocol for data collection in mental health-related research.  Our results, delivered in a fully functional Java tool, are designed for public use and aim to inspire further advancements in detecting depression from social media posts as well as other mental health disorders, laying the groundwork for future research and development in this area. This study aims to analyze the COVID-19 pandemic's impact on different age groups 
of three distinct regions:  China,  Europe, and  the United States. We use an innovative 
approach that combinescompartmental models with a unique demographic structure 
that accounts for varying age distributions across these regions. This model 
encompasses 15 distinct age groups and incorporates random variability in key 
parameters, such as infection and hospitalization rates, to better capture regional 
uncertainties. However, the model does not account for socioeconomic and ethnic 
factors that influence COVID-19 spread. This limitation allows for the potential 
integration of these factors in future refinements. 

We begin by developing a model specifically for each region but do not pursue 
predictions due to ongoing uncertainty surrounding COVID-19. Instead, we perform 
back-calculations to determine parameter values for each region. Notably, our study 
reveals that regional age structures significantly influence COVID-19 spread, 
indicating the potential for age-targeted interventions. Moreover, the variability in 
infection and hospitalization rates among regions is substantial, emphasizing the need 
for tailored public health policies in each area. 

Ultimately, this initial framework serves as a foundation for further refinement and 
expansion, allowing for the investigation of various scenarios, including the impact 
of vaccinations, different infection protocols, and potential future COVID-19 
developments. By providing a flexible model, we can explore a wide range of practical 
applications and interventions.

On one hand, classical models suggest that changes in genetics, traits, and ecology unfold at significantly different rates. To address this discrepancy, we present a new approach that reconciles these models by introducing a novel dynamic that affects the tempo of eco-evolutionary responses. However, the question remains whether SSL models are resistant to deliberate manipulation. To address this, SSL models were subjected to a range of attacks on their speech classification performance, specifically in the context of being called out for inappropriate language. The aging population in the world's languages, particularly those that are now considered historical, poses a significant challenge to linguists and researchers. As these languages continue to evolve, the number of speakers declines, putting further pressure on the existing resources available for research. This critical issue is exacerbated by the limited availability of annotated resources necessary for language research, a problem further complicated by the tendency of errors to propagate during the annotation process itself. A recent study found that approximately fifty percent of the part-of-speech annotations found in the well-known CORA10 corpus are inaccurate. In an effort to circumvent the problem of error propagation, the study proposes set-valued part-of-speech tagging as a means of representing ambiguous syntax. A novel set-valued prediction approach, known as set-based output sequence to label mapping (S2L), is presented, which enables set-valued part-of-speech annotations to be converted from approximate label sets. When tested on CORA10, the method demonstrated a significant decrease in the average Levenshtein distance to the true label set of 6.42 points, or nearly two-thirds of the original distance, with further application of the method yielding an overall S2L error rate of 8.32%. When the S2L method was used in conjunction with a neural network, the resulting error rate fell to 4.69%, representing over fifty percent reduction in the original error rate. Using CORA10 as a model, the study investigates how the quality of training data, specifically the source of annotations, affects the accuracy of part-of-speech annotations. When the study's set-valued part-of-speech annotations are used to correct the errors in the corpus, the resulting method outperforms a state-of-the-art system trained on the flawed dataset. Additionally, the study finds that utilizing a machine translation approach based on part-of-speech annotations alone can provide comparable results with minimal loss in efficiency. Ultimately, the study highlights the need for set-valued part-of-speech annotations as a means of preserving the accuracy of linguistic research despite the presence of errors in the dataset. A trusted node-based quantum error correction approach, the concealed inverses protocol (CIP), represents a distinct classification of quantum error correction methods. Unlike other approaches that directly correct errors, CIP masks quantum errors within a quantum circuit, extracts the corresponding classical errors, and uses these to restore the original quantum state. This study examines how five different single-qubit error correcting circuits, four being universal, can effectively repair quantum errors in a five-qubit superconducting quantum processor and restore a computable outcome. Furthermore, analysis of the noise characteristics of the circuits, and comparisons between the circuits and a standard quantum error correcting code, the codeword stabilized noise suppression code (CNSC), are also provided. This work verifies the feasibility of utilizing the concealed inverses protocol in a quantum computing devices such as superconducting quantum processors, provided suitable circuit design strategies are employed. Moreover, we showcase that the CIP can function with a single, versatile set of error correcting circuits, in contrast to relying on the complex method of introducing a noise suppressing code through a concatenated process. Ultimately, we illustrate that the CIP has the capacity to achieve comparable noise thresholds as noise-reducing methods like CNSC, without the associated intricacies. This work presents original research.

Recently, a framework called Oriented Convolutional Networks (OCNet) has been introduced to capture information about image orientation. In this study, a modified OCNet framework called Orientation Convolutive Networks (Acorn) was developed by replacing the traditional convolution layers with adaptive convolution layers that can accommodate different orientations. The adaptive convolution layers in Acorn consist of a tensor filter and two orthogonal vectors, which allows for the retention of circular symmetry characteristics during the process of extracting rich orientation information. Our research found that incorporating orientation information can enhance the accuracy of image classification tasks, and AcorN is a efficient method for accomplishing this. Acorn was evaluated on various datasets, including CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and ImageNet, and our results demonstrate its effectiveness. For instance, our results show that Acorn can achieve an accuracy of 93.1% or higher on the CIFAR10 dataset, even when only utilizing a single adaptive convolutional layer. Additionally, our results show that Acorn can achieve an accuracy of 80.3% or higher on the CIFAR100 dataset, even when only using two adaptive convolutional layers. Our findings reveal that the significant pp → t\bar{t} + X cross-section fluctuations due to gluon splitting into multiple light flavors substantially affect the top quark mass measurement, potentially introducing up to 580 GeV mass ambiguity. Current techniques struggle to generalize to unseen scenes and cameras due to the lack of relevant training data. To address this issue, we introduce a new method based on conditional generative models that leverages adversarial training to learn camera perspective and scene structure. However, this approach is limited by its reliance on extensive training datasets. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a new conditional diffusion model called \textit{DiffDreamer}, which learns to synthesize never-seen-before views by capitalizing on the underlying image's visual information and latent code representation. In a multi-input multi-output (MIMO) network architecture, each encoder and decoder ensemble shares the same configuration, which can lead to reduced diversity in encoder performance and hinder potential improvements from shared knowledge. As a result, the maximum achievable knowledge level is not fully realized, resulting in lower than optimal performance levels. To overcome this limitation, the MIMO structure's symmetry is dynamically adjusted through asymmetric learning, which involves assigning distinct configurations to distinct components during the training process. This is achieved by converting conventional SGD binomial distribution into a gradient-based exploration strategy that exploits existing knowledge to inform exploration, thus enhancing the mutual exchange of information between encoders. As can be seen from our experiment results, the proposed approach effectively increases model diversity, lowers the learning rate, and dramatically improves state-of-the-art semantic segmentation performance under both single-gpu and multi-gpu scenarios. Specifically, the approach resulted in performance improvements of 1.7% and 1.0% over existing benchmarks, respectively. The introduced architecture also exhibits scalability and non-IID robustness, and allows for substantial reductions in the training time by factors of 2 and 4, respectively, while maintaining consistent performance levels. Significant advancements in technology have made it possible to efficiently capture and process digital images of documents since the late 19th century. Advances in image capture technology, combined with emerging AI-based methods for document analysis, are now enabling the efficient parsing of information from digital documents without requiring manual intervention. A primary barrier to the development of these AI-based tools is the scarcity of comprehensive datasets of historical documents, which are essential for training and validating the technology. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth review of existing historical record image datasets, presenting an analysis of their composition, diversity, and potential uses. A key goal of this review is to raise awareness among the academic community about the current resources available, as well as to identify areas that require further research and development to facilitate the creation of more comprehensive datasets. By reflecting the diversity of existing research in this field, this review's scope extends beyond technical papers to incorporate the contribution of top-rated conferences in the field, with a focus on identifying relevant datasets, tools, and eigenvector scores to demonstrate their significance. A accompanying spreadsheet, available online, summarizes over one hundred datasets reviewed, enabling the community to access the information in a centralized location. Additionally, we have introduced the CHRI challenge - a new, large-scale dataset of 525 million handwritten records from the UK government's Information Age Project - as part of a competition for detecting handwritten text. To enhance motion control of complex industrial robots compared to constant velocity control, we propose a new strategy utilizing additional sensors to assess the instantaneous smoothness of the motion. A method for calculating the smoothness of a motion trajectory is developed and its effectiveness evaluated through both simulated and real-world tests on an industrial robot. Results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm enhances the smoothness of the motion, even without adjusting any parameters, and significantly improves the quality of the motion by reducing jitter when applying feedforward control for the first time. In comparison to other control methods like feedforward, feedback, feedforward plus feedback, and feedforward with friction compensation, the proposed method smooths out more of the system's dynamics, and when applied to a moving object, it enables more refined motion trajectories. In addition, the proposed algorithm allows model-free motion control, meaning it can easily adjust a robot's motion trajectory without needing to update the system's kinematic model, and it can even control a robot's motion using real-time human input, resulting in applications such as handwriting and joystick control. Overall, the proposed approach provides a practical and efficient solution for improving industrial robot motion control. The molecular continuum method efficiently resolves interactions between rigid molecules and incompressible fluids, making it beneficial for designing both molecular and fluid-based systems. This paper extends the framework of the coarse-grained molecular interaction model by integrating a multi-site approach to the quadrature method for addressing the coupling between strong molecular-facial-wall and weak fluid-wall interactions. This expansion establishes a foundational framework for the coarse-grained molecular interaction model, allowing for the integration of the multi-site quadrature method to achieve practical implementation of the molecular continuum approach. This practical implementation is demonstrated to significantly reduce computational complexity from O(N^2) to O(N) while achieving multi-site convergence. This paper also presents a practical implementation of the molecular continuum approach to address issues of fixed points and interfaces within periodic systems, incorporating the multi-site quadrature method for efficient computation. This practical implementation is further evaluated in a number of case studies, including the computation of the drag coefficient of a molecule, the optimization of the binding energy of a ligand to an enzyme, and the simulation of a droplet's interaction with a protein, revealing a range of potential applications. These case studies reveal that the molecular continuum approach to these complex computational biochemistry problems can achieve significant speedup, potentially up to two orders of magnitude, when implemented with the multi-site quadrature method. Additionally, the integration of the multi-site quadrature method to the molecular continuum approach also enables the practical implementation of the method for addressing general non-spherical walls, comprising multiple flat surfaces, without increasing the computational complexity. Consequently, the method described in this paper has the potential to efficiently compute the coupling between incompressible fluids and rigid molecules, when interaction is weak, and non-spherical surfaces, when interaction is strong. This implementation represents an important extension to the molecular continuum approach to achieve practical implementation of the method, when interaction is weak, and generalization of the quadrature method to achieve practical implementation of the method, when interaction is strong. When interaction is weak, the method described in this paper has the potential to significantly reduce computational complexity from O(N^2) to O(N), while when interaction is strong, the method described in this paper does not change the computational complexity, as it already samples the weak interaction with O(N) samples, in a coarse-grained setting. The metric dimension $\gd(G)$ of a graph $G$ is defined by the minimum number of vertices needed to determine the distance between any two vertices within $G$. In this study, we establish tight bounds or approximations for $\gd(G)$ in scenarios where the vertex feedback vertex set (FVS) has a limited size. Specifically, we show that double-exponentially many FVSs of size $k$ in a graph of maximum degree $\Delta$ require at least $\Omega\left(\frac{\Delta}{\log |\text{FVS}(G,k)|}\right)$ vertices to determine distances in $G$. We also provide an alternative bound of $\gd(G) = O\left(\frac{\Delta^2 k}{\Delta + \log |S|}\right)$ for any set $S$ of $k$ vertices in $G$ that forms an independent set. Furthermore, we prove that for graphs of diameter $D$ where a bipartite induced subgraph has a maximum degree of $d$ and a number $k$ of vertex disjoint such subgraphs, the metric dimension is given by $\gd(G) = O\left(\frac{d(k+1)}{\log(k+1)}\right) + \frac{\Delta(k+1)}{\log(k+1)}\cdot\mathbb{E}[D^2]$. We propose a polynomial-time algorithm that, given an independent set $S$ of size $k$ in a graph $G$, identifies at least $\gd(G,S) = O\left(\frac{\Delta^2 k}{\Delta + \log |S|}\right)$ vertices within $S$. We also analyze the complexity of the independent set feedback vertex set problem, showing it can be solved in logarithmic time for $k = \log |S|$ and remains hard for $k = \log |S| - 1$. We provide an alternative explanation for the known $2^{O(\log^{2}_{|S|} \log \log |S|)}$ time complexity using the Lov\'{a}sz function rather than a polynomial volume algorithm. We implement a new variant of the metric dimension parameterized by $k$ known as the $k$-metric dimension problem, which can be solved in $f(k) \cdot \log^{2.5} |S|$ time using the minimum Fortuin-Kasteleyn partition function sampling. Planets with fixed atmospheric compositions are not considered candidates for habitability, but planets with dynamic atmospheres that maintain greenhouse gases could have zones or regions suitable for liquid water and potential life. According to global climate models, these zones could potentially occur near the planet's inner boundary where temperature reaches -10 degrees Celsius, but little is known about the lower boundary limit below 0 degrees Celsius. One critical factor affecting this limit is the occurrence of episodic floods that dig deep channels in the surface of icy bodies, determining if liquid water can be sustained in their crust. To estimate how these events impact habitability, we studied these floods using a 2D planetary hydrodynamic model, simulating the lower boundary of an N2-dominated atmosphere with snowball and greenhouse states. Our model revealed that floods are likely triggered by localized errors in atmospheric calculations, developing into events that remove up to 20% of the polar ice cap ice and form new ocean areas. Upon analyzing the chemical changes resulting from these events, we discovered that atmospheric NH3 and CH4 are significantly reduced or increased, and atmospheric O2 levels are potentially driven to extinction or near habitability levels below the inner boundary limit. Our findings also imply that these events can lead to the formation of low-pressure ocean environments that could protect early atmospheres from massive gas releases, such as the giant impact that formed the Earth's moon. Overall, our research suggests that episodic floods could play a critical role in the evolution of terrestrial planets with dynamic atmospheres, determining their lower boundary limits for water-based life and potential habitability. Furthermore, our study shows that planetary science should consider not only the average habitable zones but also variable environments, such as those created by these dramatic atmospheric events. To further the understanding of these processes, we recommend integrating the planetary hydrodynamic model with a more detailed model of interior chemistry and geochemistry that accounts for the complex interactions between atmospheric, solid Earth, and liquid water components. By exploring these interactions in the context of these atmospheric giants, we may uncover new insights into the habitability of these planets and potential analogues in our solar system. Our combined model, the EPIC model, is developed to investigate these interactions and identify key factors that determine habitability and the evolution of these environments. By implementing this model and pursuing this research, we aim to identify the critical components that affect the habitability of planets with dynamic atmospheres and variable environments. In typical materials, the intensity of the screen decreases inversely in proportion to the distance from the source of the force or charge and logarithmically increases with time. In contrast, our research on granular materials reveals a unique screening mechanism, where the intensity of the screen decreases exponentially with distance and is unaffected by the passage of time, yielding an extremely high screening constant. To confirm our theoretical findings, we conducted an experiment where two adjacent columns of granular towers were electrified at different intervals, and by measuring the exchange of electric charge across the columns, we demonstrated the existence of an extremely high screening constant. To verify the time independence of the screening mechanism, we performed another experiment that utilized the technique of radioactive tracing to monitor the flow of particles between columns. Upon confirming our initial assumptions through these experiments, we developed a computational model that mimics the real-world conditions by simulating the process of grain flow between two columns using the Discrete Element Method. Our study offers the first validation of the anomalous screening theory in a specific mechanism and has the potential to cause a significant revolution in the understanding of screening mechanisms. Ultimately, our research may lead to the discovery of novel mechanisms for information transfer and may even be utilised in applications such as information dense technologies.
