The Rapid Multipole Method effectively simulates the interaction between N bodies and a point source of mass by replacing the source with a multipole expansion, however this approach typically does not account for the conservation of angular momentum in the simulated point source mass structure. We introduce an enhanced version of the Rapid Multipole Method that maintains the angular momentum of the embedded sub-system, thus allowing for the accurate simulation of sub-structures such as star clusters within larger galactic potentials. We modify the standard process using either a quaternion based reconstruction or re-evalution of the Hamiltonian to ensure angular momentum conservation. Our results show that the modified method preserves angular momentum in ideal scenarios, and we demonstrate a method to quantify the amount of angular momentum error introduced in each time step. We find that the re-evaluation method preserves at least 99.9% of the initial angular momentum in ideal scenarios, and typically achieves conservation of 100% of the initial angular momentum in real-world runs of N-body simulations. This enhanced method also effectively maintains the overall angular momentum of the surrounding galactic potential as well as the surrounding galactic potential's outer quadrupole and higher order multipole moments. We provide a series of benchmark simulations to illustrate the methodology and demonstrate its application in a galactic potential with a nested star cluster merger. These benchmarks show that the modified method prevents unwanted interactions between the embedded star cluster and the surrounding galactic potential's outer multipole moments as well as prevents the embedded star cluster from affecting the galactic potential's overall angular momentum. We obtain significantly better conservation of angular momentum in the simulated run compared to the standard Rapid Multipole Method. These results imply that the modified method is suitable for a wide-range of astrophysical simulations including the integration of multiple nested sub-structures within larger galactic potentials. The modified method will thus allow for the accurate and efficient simulation of a diverse range of astrophysical systems such as galactic clusters, galaxies and galaxy sized halos. The integration of this methodology with other conservative integrators such as tree code and other methods for modeling galactic potentials will further expand the scope of astrophysical simulations in the near future. The modified method described in this document has already been effectively integrated into the N-body code "HIGNS" and previously integrated into the AMUSE software library. This study explores the complexities of identifying hate-speech in complex languages through a detailed analysis of a large neural network's performance on Hindi and Bengali. The inherent difficulty of modeling these languages, exacerbated by the scarcity of available data, is compounded by the need for linguistic representations that can effectively capture the context of textual hate-speech content. To address these challenges, a novel neural framework is proposed, incorporating an encoder, classifier, and connector modules, all working in tandem to identify hate-speech in two prominent Indo-European languages. The reliability of this model is established through the inclusion of an exhaustive examination of its internal components. Furthermore, the model's performance is compared to that of a state-of-the-art system, highlighting the significance of examining low-accuracy predictions to refine hate-speech detection models, especially when working within linguistic and data constraints common to low-resourced languages. The model's performance was evaluated using two classifications, the first being a static approach with a training set of 17,054 classifications, and the second being a dynamic approach with a training set of 13,319 classifications. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of an advanced neural framework in the precise identification of hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali, two particularly challenging languages. The study also showcases an original analysis of its internal components, and highlights the importance of examining the low-accuracy predictions of hate-speech detection models. The model's source code is available for public access on the GitHub platform at the following link: https://github.com/01116717/Hate-Speech-Neural-Net. The study also involved a transfer of the model's capabilities to another low-resourced Indian language, Hindi. The results of this study reveal that the incorporation of an additional neural connection can serve as an efficient method for adapting the model to other languages, thus broadening its applicability in the field of hate-speech identification. The study also makes the publication available in Hindi for better understanding. Notably, our model's outcomes were unbiased, as assessed by a new metric called Normalized Anti-Knowledge Gradient. This method makes it possible to explain the model's decisions and identifies the key factors that contribute to the prediction of manual skills. Overall, our study provides an efficient solution to the issue of manual ability prediction in the commercial driving industry, and highlights the significance of using expert supervision as a critical component of the machine learning process. This approach has the potential to support the development of fair and reliable models for assessing commercial driving manual skills. This research introduces a novel numerical approach, the outward complex scaling method. It employs a time-scale transformation, accompanied by a real-space scaling of the atomic or molecular coordinates. Similar to the Broadening Complex Scaling Method, the outward scaling method effectively circumvents the continuum threshold problem by utilizing a first-order Lagrange multiplier. A comprehensive theoretical framework for this method is developed, including proof of its applicability to the Schrödinger equation and a systematic expansion of its underlying perturbation theory around the scaled configuration. Furthermore, a study examining the energy levels of hydrogen-like ions in strong DC fields provides a thorough validation of the method's efficacy. All calculations presented utilize the outward scaling method in conjunction with a finite-element numerical solver. It successfully reproduces well-converged energy results for various 1s states of hydrogen-like ions in both weak and strong DC fields, including a critical examination of the method's dependence on the imaginary scaling parameter. Additionally, a comprehensive investigation into the autoionization transition widths of 1s states in hydrogen-like ions provides insight into the effect of the scaling method on non-hermitian physics. Importantly, this approach does not preclude the imaginary part of the energy, explicitly enabling the calculation of physical quantities related to the width of autoionization transitions. A comparison with existing literature values demonstrates the method's capability to produce highly accurate results for various parameters. Lastly, a theoretical foundation for the application of the outward scaling method to the multi-configurational self-consistent field equation is laid out, with a view to expanding the method's capabilities to accurately solve more complex problems. A future outlook on future applications and adaptations of the method is proposed. The outward scaling method presents a versatile numerical approach that could be adapted to address a broad range of challenges in quantum physics, including the theoretical interpretation of recent experiments on hydrogen-like ions in strong DC fields and historic observations of non-hermitian physics in three dimensions. The goal of this research is to address a complex challenge involving approximate matching of time series. The initial step involves generating a compact representation of a time series, which then allows for the creation of a data structure that can efficiently determine closest neighbors. Building upon existing research in this area, this study aims to establish the minimum required precision for achieving high-quality approximate matches by exploiting the series' intrinsic characteristics. Two such constraints are derived in this study, which jointly suggest that achieving optimal results may be computationally impractical. The existing research in this area is further bolstered by experimental results demonstrating its practical implications, and a related problem is also explored, which involves expanding the scope of potential applications to multi-dimensional data. The investigation of this problem reveals that the concept of estimates must be introduced in order to facilitate efficient processing of closest neighbor searches. The development of novel algorithms and the evaluation of their performance in terms of precision and speed are also key components of this study, which ultimately seeks to contribute to the understanding of this area through a combination of theoretical and practical insights. Theoretical limitations of this research are established, specifically that the application of exact distances may be necessary to achieve high-quality approximate matches in certain scenarios. The proposed techniques are evaluated in terms of false positive rates, which are determined through a comprehensive analysis of a dataset comprised of diverse time series. The incorporation of post-processing techniques, which involve additional calculations to verify match quality, is also explored, despite theoretical limitations that render such techniques impractical. The depth of insight gained in this study is reflected in the proposed performance guarantees, specifically an upper bound of false positive rate of 0.05 after applying a two-stage verification process. In various fields, such as physics, biology, and medicine, high-precision measurements are crucial but often hindered by measurement errors. While measurement devices can't eliminate errors, a promising approach called measurement error reduction has gained momentum. HER, a highly effective and widely applied method, achieves nearly optimal outcomes but comes with a significant drawback - it can only process a set number of data points at a time. We introduce a comprehensive framework, called expandable HER, or eHER, which allows the results to be scaled up to accommodate any quantity of data without limit. Our eHER framework achieves this by breaking down the data into manageable chunks, applying HER to each, and collating the outcomes. To ensure the integrity of the results, we envelop eHER within an iterative Bayesian unraveling framework, or eIBRU. eIBRU uses a bespoke Bayesian model to help eHER determine the extent of the errors and, thus, choose the optimal sample size. Our comprehensive testing reveals that eIBRU outperforms not just the basic eHER method but also the basic HER in complex scenarios. Furthermore, eIBRU has real-world applications - we demonstrate its efficacy in the determination of the Einstein-Gravitational Constant, a highly complex operation within the scope of the work. As more diverse robots operate in the same workspace, the issue of interpersonal communication emerges. A robot's ability to express intentions through visual indications is investigated as a means of communicating with users, particularly those from different cultural backgrounds. Insights from human factors research reveal that intentions can be conveyed through two standards: action-based norms, such as completing a task, and expectation-based norms, such as adhering to rules. However, these norms are often culturally relative. To address this, a decision theory-based model called the Expectation-Action Transformer, comprising two modules that jointly predict action-based and expectation-based norms, is developed and tested. Results show that this model can express more nuanced norms than either the action-based model or expectation-based model alone, and it performs as well as a human observer in similar scenarios. This research presents the first attempt at using decision theory to convey multiple norms to humans, and it achieves comparable results to human perception. This research aims to contribute to the development of collaborative robots that can interact with diverse people by establishing consistent standards of behavior. In tasks such as delivery or maintenance, robots may need to travel between numerous destinations with varying levels of familiarity. To enhance their navigation skills for unfamiliar areas, we have developed a data representation framework that outlines a region's layout in a hierarchical fashion. By using a map of the region's overall topology and detailed topological maps of local areas, this system enables robots to efficiently travel between unknown destinations. To better understand these maps, we have created a set of standardized symbols that represent different local features. Furthermore, we have established rules for combining these symbols into a coherent overall topology map. Through experiments in a simulated environment, we have demonstrated that our navigation system is effective and efficient, traveling on average 20% closer to its goal in unfamiliar settings. We employ the Dyson equation to investigate a gapless Rashba gas in a narrow, hollow wire, modeling its behavior in a nanoscale concave shape. By reducing the gap size, we simulate a transition from a discrete surface-plasmon mode to a gapless, three-dimensional Rashba gapped mode. This transformation is characterized by a substantial shift in the surface-plasmon charge density from the edges to the center of the wire. As the gap size approaches zero, the surface-plasmon energy converges to a finite value, unlike the charge density which tends to a delta-function. These findings demonstrate that the three-dimensional Rashba gapped mode has a finite energy and substantial electron spill-over effect. However, this behavior is overlooked when only considering a quasi-one-dimensional wire using the Thomas-Fermi approximation and hydrodynamic model. We also observe that the electron spill-over and nonlocality enhance the surface-plasmon energy, revealing their profound influence on the three-dimensional Rashba gapped mode. Furthermore, our research highlights the need for a higher-dimensional description and a nonperturbative approach to uncover the properties of gapless Rashba gases in nanoscale systems. Finally, the concept of quasi-localized gapped modes and quasi-particles is explored, with implications for observation in experiments. The present theory and results provide significant insights for designing and analyzing nanoscale gapped modes in three-dimensional systems. An entity's presence or absence is then fed back to the model during the extraction process, providing the model with further information to enhance its accuracy. In medical settings, clinicians often face challenges when processing the large volumes of information available to each patient. This consideration of multiple factors is crucial in identifying comorbidities and providing comprehensive, data-driven suggestions. However, the complexity of medical data and the need for diverse comparisons can make it difficult to identify similar patients. To address this, a novel graph neural network model called DGNN has been developed for predictive healthcare tasks. This model utilizes a similarity graph that aggregates global information about patients, doctors, and organizations to facilitate comparative analysis at a larger scale. By leveraging diverse similarity links, the model is capable of identifying similar patients for predictive tasks such as identifying comorbidities and generating personalized recommendations. To optimize computational efficiency, a strategy of approximating graph representations with a mixture of patient attributes has been employed. The potential of DGNN lies in its extendability to various deep learning architectures and scalability to large datasets, opening up new possibilities for its application in real-world medical settings. Experimental results using a large dataset from 2.8 million patients have shown the efficacy of the model in tackling complex medical data and its potential to improve predictive accuracy and outcomes. With the growing popularity of digital health initiatives, the model is poised to play a significant role in leveraging digital health data to inform clinical decision-making in the future. The code for the model is publicly available for non-commercial use at https://github.com/harshm121/dgnn.

Geolocation systems can be particularly useful in outdoor settings, incorporating a combination of sensor data, including the camera's field of view and the orientation of the device. We aim to improve the precision of geolocation calculations by reducing the influence of biased information. To achieve this goal, we have developed a method for correcting biased input by creating a filter based on deep neural networks. Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is an essential procedure that healthcare professionals use for assessing patients' condition and tracking the progression of the disease. Recent advancements in deep learning have led to the creation of multiple MS segmentation pipelines, each with its unique characteristics. These models, despite their success, were typically trained separately and weren't designed to adapt gradientually to sequential patient data as it's progressively collected in clinical settings. We investigate the potential of incorporating ongoing learning with existing deep learning models to improve their adaptation to see MS lesions in sequential patient data as they're diagnosed over time. We observed that our proposed continuous learning strategy led to the reduction of re-training the model when interpreting new imaging data for previously established patients from 80-100% to 20-60%. Nonetheless, the outcome wasn't directly reflected in the segmentation accuracy of the model. Importantly, the concept of continuous learning in the field of medical image analysis remains relatively unexplored, and further research is required in identifying the suitable factors that contribute to the effective adaptation of the models to the ever-growing information of the patients. Furthermore, we recommend conducting rigorous evaluations to ensure that the continuous learning of the models doesn't compromise their dependability and robustness. Continual learning, in the long run, led to the precise prediction of lesions at half the time spent training from scratch, in conjunction with the analysis of the dynamics of the models and the potential for the catastrophic forgetting of the initial knowledge on the segmentation of the MS lesions to be successfully counteracted. A new comparative concept is introduced, referred to as dual comparison, where the focus lies on discovering shared properties held by two elements within a set possessing such properties in common, rather than emphasizing differences. Dual comparison is exemplified through case studies including the dual comparison of data sets, concepts, and methods. Importantly, it is highlighted that dual comparison can occur at various levels, encompassing not only individual elements but also collective entities such as conferences and fields of research. Moreover, through an examination of the 2020 Computational Social Sciences conference, an investigation is conducted to identify the shared characteristics of the elements within this category, as part of a dual comparison of events focused on interdisciplinary approaches. Another example demonstrates how a dual comparison of fields can reveal the shared traits associated with data science. Furthermore, a dual comparison of CSA journals aims to identify the common attributes of these publications. Finally, through a dual comparison of STC's technical areas, an attempt is made to determine the shared characteristics of the elements within this domain.

High-density regions in the early universe, particularly those that form early stars and galaxies, also have a high probability of collapsing into primordial black holes. If these black holes make up a significant portion of the universe's mass, they could potentially replace dark energy as its dominant component. We ran a series of simulations in the MERGER project to study how different types of early universe structures influence the formation of black holes, examining either numerous small black holes or fewer massive ones, while comparing them to models that appear smooth on a cosmic scale. Our results highlighed the importance of further investigation into the characteristics of early galaxy formation in order to better understand the potential for primordial black holes as a dark energy candidate. We utilized the PopSyCLE code in the MERGER project to conduct these studies. The code simulates galaxy evolution to estimate where and when early galaxy formation occurs, which helps in creating models of black hole formation. These models can then be compared to observations of the universe today to determine whether primordial black holes could be a viable option for dark energy. The implementation of different black hole formation options in the code is also explained.

To alleviate some of this expense, alternative adjustment methods have been developed that are more efficient in terms of parameters, such as learning only the adjustment layer or using pre-trained positions as fixed references. Nevertheless, these methods may still struggle to effectively learn about sentence meanings, hindering their performance in complex cases. To overcome these limitations, we introduced a distinct token adaptation method as a compromise between efficiency and effectiveness, which allows the adjustment model to learn about sentence meanings at a lower computational cost. Our experiments on six datasets reveal that our approach outperforms comparable methods in adjusting for LMs and achieves superior results in various downstream tasks, even surpassing the efficacy of conventional fine-tuning. Notably, our analysis confirms the importance of unique token adaptation in achieving accurate word composition and demonstrates its potential as a plausible alternative to fine-tuning for LMs. To facilitate future research, we have made our code and data available for public access. When considering a context-free preference ordering, every item is viewed as a standalone option. In contrast, a contextual preference ordering takes into account the interdependence of items, similar to how people prefer summer with hiking and winter with skiing. As such, contextual preferences can more accurately reflect real-world preferences, especially in set addition problems where the value of combining two sets depends on the context. However, contextual preference ordering faces the challenge of efficiently processing queries. In this paper, a new problem called PHIAL is proposed to address set addition issues, and a more general framework with three related problems is developed for further exploration. By designing these problems, a more comprehensive understanding of contextual preference ordering is achieved, and a significant difference in computational complexity between contextual and non-contextual preference ordering is revealed, specifically a lower bound of quasi-polynomial for 3-LABEL PHIAL and an exponential lower bound for non-contextual solutions in SET ADDITION. Moreover, a new algorithm with an improved complexity is developed for PHIAL, outperforming existing algorithms for set addition problems by achieving a 2^(Omega(log n / log b)) time complexity. Additionally, a more general algorithm with a 2^(Omega(n)) time complexity for all 3-LABEL XSET ADDITION problems is developed. In order to analyze the computational complexity of contextual preference ordering, a new notion with size and depth is introduced for the input size, and a hierarchy of problems with a higher complexity and a lower depth is carefully designed. As input size increases, a more complex problem is encountered, and a specific threshold of input size is found where the computational complexity of contextual and non-contextual solutions to SET ADDITION and PHIAL diverge. In summary, a new framework with a higher computational complexity for contextual preference ordering has been developed, and a more accurate analysis of the input size of set addition problems with a higher complexity and a lower depth has been achieved. The developed algorithm for PHIL with a 2^(Omega(log n / log b)) time complexity outperforms existing algorithms for set addition problems, and a more comprehensive understanding of the input size of contextual preference ordering has been achieved. A new concept of interactive complexity has been introduced, and a more complex problem of interactive complexity with an exponential lower bound for non-interactive solutions is identified. A more accurate analysis of the input size of interactive complexity for contextual preference ordering has been achieved, and a higher computational complexity for interactive solutions to PHIL and 3-LABEL SET ADDITION problems has been confirmed. Our study examines the origin and expression of the heat capacity ratio in relation to the configurational entropy and internal energy of glass-forming polymer liquids. Through various theoretical and simulation methods, we found that the heat capacity ratio is sensitive to the temperature-driven disruption of the liquid's structural arrangements. Additionally, at temperatures near the liquidus point, the thermodynamic stability of these structures has a significant influence on the heat capacity ratio. Conversely, the entropic and energetic heat capacities, which account for the disorder of the liquid, correlate inversely with the heat capacity ratio. These findings are crucial in understanding how the heat capacity ratio facilitates the prediction of the liquid's thermodynamic and kinetic glassiness characteristics. Furthermore, we identified a crucial heat capacity divergence as the nominal freezing point, indicating a thermodynamic instability in the liquid at that temperature. Our results also demonstrated that the heat capacity ratio can be used to estimate the liquidus point while accounting for the effects of high-temperature structural disorder and liquidus deviation on its value. Finally, the relationship between the heat capacity ratio and configurational entropy was found to be non-linear, particularly at low temperatures, due to the influence of the second-order liquid-solid transition on the configurational entropy. Our study provides new insights into the heat capacity ratio and its role in understanding glass formation. It also expands our knowledge of its connections to the entropic and energetic heat capacities, the structural and kinetic characteristics of glass-forming liquids, and the thermodynamic-dynamic relationships in polymer liquids. These connections have been explored in relation to the liquid's structural and dynamic features in various conditions. One key challenge for sophisticated language models is learning to recognize and process sentences that logically contradict each other, a capability that we call denial processing. To address this challenge, we've developed a new method that exploits the leading context of contradictory sentences to identify cases of logical conflict. Our approach is founded on the principle that words have different semantic meanings when it comes to denying them, and that this contrast can be exploited to identify cases of logical conflict. We've tested this approach within the context of transformer language models, and found that incorporating denial processing enhances the accuracy of models predicting whether two given sentences are contradictory. Our approach results in improvement of consistency score from 56% to 82%, and opens up possibilities for a range of applications requiring denial processing capability. We've also discovered that our algorithm can be scaled down to a simplified version that only increases computation by a factor of 2, making it more suitable for a mobile setting. In the majority of neural machine translation (NMT) models, variables are updated based on past observations, which can result in an inconsistent production order. This paper presents a novel Look-forward Attention model that incorporates future observations into variable updates, maintaining a coherent production order. It is notable that localized interface information is only available at the decoding stage, making it necessary to innovate an attention mechanism that can look ahead to the future. This model is specifically designed for the production framework, as explored in earlier studies. Interestingly, even with a limited lookahead of just one word, the model showed a notable improvement, achieving a 3.05 and 4.23 BLEU points increase on the JMT10 and NIST06 Arabic - English datasets respectively, when compared to the renowned Transformer interface. This notable achievement suggests that future-oriented attention has the potential to enhance NMT performance significantly. Furthermore, the model demonstrates the ability to mitigate Halluzinations commonly observed in production-based NMT systems. It is expected that future-oriented attention may have applications and improvements in other studies as well. The source code for the Look-forward Attention model proposed in this production-based NMT study is available on GitHub: https://github.com/linguistics-sot/LAprod. Moreover, the model's integration with other NMT interfaces reveals the potential for substantial generalization, suggesting that future-oriented attention has the potential to greatly enhance NMT performance. When training the Look-forward Attention model without incorporating production in its loss function, it showed a 6.04 and 6.75 BLEU points improvement on the NIST06 and JMT10 datasets respectively, when compared to the renowned Transformer interface. This notable achievement suggests that future-oriented attention has the potential to greatly enhance NMT performance and that further investigation is necessary. When incorporating production in its loss function, the model shows even more substantial improvements, 10.18 and 14.75 BLEU points increase on the NIST06 and JMT10 datasets respectively, indicating very promising results. It is expected that future work may further reinforce the impact of future-oriented attention in NMT. When used exclusively, the Look-forward Attention model shows excellent performance and a notable decrease in Halluzinations. Utilizing both hydromagnetic and magnetohydrodynamic frameworks, our study investigates how geostrophic beta dynamo theory aligns with modern concepts of magnetohydrodynamics.  We demonstrate that the emergence of the small-scale magnetic field in a laminar convection-driven global dynamo requires direct influence from turbulent processes, such as magnetic diffusivity and velocity helicity, in addition to traditional mean-field parameters like thermal diffusivity and baroclinicity.  Furthermore, our exploration of various parameter regimes reveals that the simplifications inherent to mean-field frameworks and global shell models do not always permit an exhaustive understanding of the dynamo process, as they potentially mask necessary turbulent influences.  Ultimately, our analysis highlights the significance of reflecting upon the underlying magnetohydrodynamics and available numerical techniques in the pursuit of uncovering the mysteries of global convective dynamos.

The intergalactic medium within low-mass galaxies remains a poorly understood area of study. Research has demonstrated that some dwarf satellite galaxies of the Milky Way exhibit X-ray emissions, likely originating from hot gas within the galaxies themselves or the surrounding hot intergalactic medium. However, the exact characteristics of this gas are unknown, including its temperature, mass, and whether it is confined to the galaxies or part of the larger halo. To address these questions, we have studied a sample of 15 dwarf satellites using Chandra's X-ray data, collecting more than 1 million seconds of observation time. Our analysis reveals that gas temperatures range from $0.5-3.0 \times 10^7$ K and mass from $10^8- 10^9$ M$_\odot$. We cannot determine the source of the gas due to a lack of data on the gas's pressure. The observed gas temperatures are higher than those of the Milky Way's halo, leading to several possible explanations including higher temperatures within gas clouds, slower radiative cooling, or the presence of active star formation or nuclear activity. We hypothesize that this gas may be a characteristic feature of dwarf satellite galaxies. Our findings have implications for understanding gas dynamics and chemistry within these galaxies, potential interactions with the Milky Way's intergalactic medium, and the role of feedback on the gas. Our analysis also highlights the importance of identifying the primary source of the gas through follow-up observations and simulations. In particular, we suggest conducting a deep observation of the globular cluster $\omega$ Centauri, which has a X-ray luminosity similar to M31's M33, using the XMM-Newton observatory to determine if the gas originates from within the galaxy or the surrounding IGM. Such a study could have far-reaching implications for understanding dwarf galaxy gas dynamics and chemistry. Ultimately, our understanding of dwarf satellite galaxy gas dynamics, chemistry, feedback, and other related processes remains incomplete, much like their high-mass counterparts. Our extensive Chandra dataset has brought us closer to understanding gas temperatures and masses within low-mass galaxies but left us guessing about the gas's pressure. To close this knowledge gap, we need more observational data and simulations that account for the complex interactions between gas, stars, and feedback processes across mass scales. Our present study, though limited in scope, has a broader objective: to bolster a new era of interdisciplinary research that integrates a greater understanding of galaxy gas dynamics, chemistry, feedback, and related astrophysical and cosmological processes. Utilizing crowdsourcing platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk to create high-quality text summaries is a complex challenge. We discovered that only around 8% of Turkers demonstrate the necessary skills for decent quality, and because they participate in tasks on a temporary basis, they do so without a long-term commitment or loyalty. Given these obstacles, identifying and reassembling a reliable team of summarizers for a particular project proves a difficult task. This paper investigates the process of hiring a competent team of summary writers by first developing a series of assessment tasks that evaluate a worker's understanding of summarization principles. By adjusting the selection process and varying the composition of the assessment tasks, we were able to identify and retain 30% to 45% of the original participating Turkers as a reliable team of summarizers with consistently high scores. We discovered that by retaining three levels of high-scoring workers, we were able to identify teams capable of producing high-quality summaries, and in some instances, equivalent to those created by humans. Our study demonstrates the process of creating a stable team of summarizers as a feasible approach, and the resulting summaries show promise of meeting human quality standards. Nonetheless, it remains a complicated process to establish such a team, and further refinement is required to enhance the likelihood of recruiting and retaining high-quality summarizers, and ultimately, developing summaries as good as those created by humans. We observed, however, that the lower the quality expected for a summary, the simpler it is to recruit and retain a competent team. This enables the creation of teams capable of producing good, though not excellent, summaries with stability. We discovered that certain assessment tasks are more successful in evaluating a worker's ability to create high-quality summaries than others, and we identified two key factors that determine the success of an assessment task: its actual test validity, and the level of selection difficulty. Ultimately, our study opens the door for developing a method to locate and retain a competent team of summarizers, and encourages the importance of validity in the assessment process. This is critical when hiring workers on a crowdsourcing platform where, unlike traditional employment settings, the concept of continued work and loyalty is uncommon. Text-video retrieval has become a prominent research area within multimedia analysis due to the rapid expansion of digital content across multiple media platforms. Current methods that deal with overlapping visual and textual information for video comprehension often adopt a cross-modal attention framework. Nevertheless, existing approaches suffer from several limitations: the constrained input representation due to fixed-size token embedding; the complex and less efficient token matching process, which depends on attention scores; and the biased video representation resulting from the inherent nature of self-attention layers. To address these issues, a novel retrieval model called TS2-Net has been introduced. It stands out by featuring a versatile token shifting mechanism and a custom token matching layer, which efficiently selects crucial cues from videos under inquiry. Furthermore, TS2-Net incorporates a different transformer model, distinct from the original VL-BERT, which contributes to the development of a universal video understanding model. Through comprehensive experiments conducted on various benchmark datasets, such as MSRVTT, VATEX, ActivityNet, and DiDeMo, TS2-Net exhibits superior retrieval performance when compared to the latest state-of-the-art models. An important observation made during these experiments reveals that MSRVTT's well-adapted, tightly-packeted video sequences tend to underperform when analyzed using TS2-Net, which highlights a need for further research on text-video retrieval from dynamically structured video content. Implementation details of TS2-Net, along with associated data and source code, are available on GitHub. An execution overhead of approximately 3.5 times relative to the top-performing VL-BERT model was observed, which demonstrates the potential of incorporating TS2-Net's novel token shifting and token matching operations to further enhance text-video retrieval performance. Ultimately, a hybrid approach combining the understanding of MSRVTT's structured video content with the incorporation of TS2-Net's novel operations holds the potential to propel the development of highly accurate text-video retrieval models. A future research goal will involve extending TS2-Net to the recently introduced DiDeMo dataset containing video clips annotated by numerical data, with potential applications in computational semiotics and the discovery of hidden patterns within media content. Research will also involve the development of a universal text-video retrieval model capable of performing equally well on various challenging video datasets. A key goal of this project will consist of integrating TS2-Net with cutting-edge text and vision analysis models, which may lead to breakthroughs in the areas of computational semiotics, biological and consumer behavior analysis, as well as other domains requiring accurate text-video retrieval. A measure algebra is said to have the locally normal property if for every measure on a standard measure algebra with a subset that forms a subalgebra, this subset must equal the entire algebra. This article investigates the conditions under which a measure algebra exhibits the locally normal property. It is proven that a measure algebra is locally normal if and only if it can be compared to a specific, countable algebra. This countable algebra can be thought of as the completion of the minimal algebra for measures of finite or infinite measure. The article also explores how the locally normal property relates to other characteristics of a measure algebra and includes examples to illustrate the different conditions. Furthermore, it is shown that a measure algebra with locally finite or infinite measure can be embedded into a larger, locally normal algebra. This article addresses two specific cases in more detail. It demonstrates that a measure algebra with locally finite measure cannot have two distinct subalgebras where one is strictly larger, unless those subalgebras encompass the entire algebra. Similarly, it is proven that a measure algebra with locally infinite measure cannot have two distinct subalgebras unless those subalgebras encompass the entire algebra. These two cases involve the minimal and completion of the minimal algebra for measures of finite or infinite measure respectively. When working on software projects, developers often encounter a range of unpleasant smells in their daily code navigation. Failing to address these smells can lead to the propagation of defects, making it harder to fix them as the code evolves. Despite the potential consequences, little is known about developers' reactions to discovering smells during code review. To this end, we conducted an online survey with 171 software developers, asking them about their responses to encountering different levels of odors during code reviews. The results show that developers strongly disagree that smells are an acceptable presence in code and consistently rate various odors as severe issues. Interestingly, while the perceived severity of smells does vary slightly with their intensity, the resulting cognitive and emotional strain remains consistent. These findings imply that developers view higher intensity smells as more severe but also as more manageable. When the smell intensity does not affect perceived difficulty, the varied cognitive strain of smells is compensated for by developers' emotional responses. These results contribute to the understanding of developer behavior when encountering smells, which can inform the creation of more effective smells detection and elimination strategies. The empirical findings also suggest that an average developer spends around 15 minutes daily to fix a smell during code review. Interestingly, developers are more likely to detect and address smells if they receive a relevant email notification. To facilitate more effective smells detection, we found that 55% of developers consider regular code review a crucial benefit in identifying smells. A recent approach, Distributed Optimal Transport (DOT), circumvents transportation planning's computational limitations by breaking it down into simpler distance matrix calculations. Although DOT is limited to few hundreds of points, we propose a deep learning framework that applies DOT's strategy to achieve high-quality representations from large-scale data in DOT-based tasks. The framework combines a deep encoder with a distributed memory block for approximate solutions to large-scale OT problems. The results demonstrate that our method delivers competitive solutions to state-of-the-art methods in tasks involving multi-mixture vision, and it also enables the extension of DOT to complex Riemannian OT problems. Moreover, the framework facilitates the use of scalable OT-based learning methods on large datasets. The source code is available at https://github.com/aliqiu/dotdeep.

In various fields, citizen participation in data-driven initiatives has shown significant benefits, and similar projects emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic, encouraging individuals to share their recent contacts to aid the nationwide contact tracing effort. These local initiatives may have greater influence due to their focus on minimal areas, allowing closer inspection of their impact. This paper involves an experimental campaign with 1,584 participants to investigate the impact of a specific local contact tracing effort in England, examining its effects on the number of self-isolated contacts and the overall success rate of the contact tracing system. The survey revealed that people willing to share their contacts were 8.7% more likely to have done so, compared to the minimal local initiative. Notably, a substantial 44% of the study's participants agreed to share their information without being prompted to do so initially. This campaign provided 207 instances of COVID-19 infection-related data. Our analysis revealed that people willing to share their information for the local and minimal initiatives reported, on average, 2.2 and 1.7 self-isolated contacts, respectively. The data also indicated a notable opposition to sharing sensitive information, particularly with external sources, where individuals were 47% more likely to resist such requests. This research provides valuable insights for the planning of future similar initiatives, where targets are defined based on geographical areas instead of numbers. These insights include the need to maintain confidentiality and transparency about the purpose of the initiative, especially when dealing with sensitive personal data. Additionally, results indicate that trust in the government's abilities and transparency about the pandemic's management can have a considerable effect on the success of similar contact tracing efforts. Automating the adjustment of an eye-in-hand camera setup in robotics poses a significant challenge due to the vast number of possible configurations. We propose an innovative method that leverages deep learning to optimize the camera's position and orientation by analyzing a single 2D image captured by an external camera or sensor. This approach involves generating simulated 3D images of an workspace using a model-based technique and then calculating the optimal camera orientation by matching a 2D scene snapshot to one of these 3D perspectives. The performance of this technique is evaluated in a real-world setting using a robotic arm. Experimental results indicate that our model accurately determines the necessary camera adjustments in the majority (70%) of cases. We also observed that our model performs better or similarly to traditional boundary-based and direct visual feedback methods in 40% and 35% of cases respectively. Furthermore, our approach enables the camera to capture the rear workspace regions that are previously inaccessible using traditional techniques. While human intervention is still sometimes necessary due to the limited capacity of our model, we found that it requires consultation of simulation-based data in only 27% of cases. We investigate certain aspects of a multiplicative stochastic process subject to a sample-dependent lower bound, and also explore the long-term behavior of a related iterative process. Ultimately, the purpose of this study is to identify conditions under which these processes converge uniformly toward positive limits, while also illustrating potential applications in probability theory, such as deriving asset price models and evaluating the efficacy of a random strategy in a game. Our method of analysis relies on establishing relationships between proposed convergence candidates and solutions to related equations, and in doing so, we demonstrate the feasibility of employing both iterative and probabilistic approaches in this investigation. Specifically, one significant finding of this study involves the derivation of a multiplicative stochastic process that converges toward a positive limit, alongside an accompanying asset price model grounded in this convergence. Additionally, another key discovery illustrates the efficacy of a proposed 'winning' strategy in a probabilistic game, characterized by its application of the 'least lucky' principle. A thorough mathematical analysis (comprising approximately 45% of this article) enables the evaluation of the average returns on such a strategy over arbitrary timeframes. As might be expected, the outcomes of this analysis vary according to the time interval in question, with periods of prosperity alternately intermingled with periods of decline. A strategic approach to playing the game could potentially be informed by a semi-logistic rule, where sample-dependent adjustments are made to a universal strategy in a manner that is beneficial to players who are "least lucky". Our method of analysis (though not the strategy itself) is applicable to a diverse range of multiplicative stochastic processes, while our study primarily focuses on cases where said processes are grounded in geometric Brownian motion, with a lower bound determined by a power law and a constant factor. There is currently a gap in our understanding of the relationship between the depth of a quantum circuit and its ability to approximate expectations of complex states. Our research demonstrates that deep circuits are not needed to obtain such approximations, as we successfully model expectation assessment for single-qubit states using shallow circuits. Specifically, we designed a set of low-depth circuits that can differentiate expectations of single-qubit states with a minimum number of quantum circuits, independent of the system size. Our findings also highlight key application scenarios where these shallow circuits can be useful, such as in chemical simulations and drug screening processes, where we demonstrate the feasibility of performing these tasks using just a few qubits and a low number of quantum circuits. Additionally, we explored the role of symmetry in these shallow circuits and found that certain situations with high symmetry allow us to reduce the number of required circuits. Lastly, we set up a framework for the classification of states using different numbers of quantum circuits and leverage this framework to better understand the trade-offs between sampling efficiency and computational resources. Our SAGE toolkit, which is built upon the Stateful Quantum Simulator, allows for the efficient implementation of these shallow circuits and provides a practical solution for the differential calculation of state expectations. Our research concludes by outlining key future research directions inspired by these findings. Our SAGE implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/ericuwinograd/shallow-shades. Our results were significantly improved through collaborations at UMass Boston, UMass Amherst, IBM, Torontonian Geometry, University of Göttingen, University of Innsbruck, and University of Leeds. Specifically, initial improvements were discovered in the cost of the universal universal fewLocalExpectation circuit, the sampling cost of the 2qBilinski circuit, and the total cost of the full 4qFermi circuit. These findings are available at https://umass.edu. All experiments were conducted using Stateful Quantum Simulator (https://stateful-quantum-simulator.github.io). The DSII equation is known for its role in modeling weakly nonlinear, strongly dispersive deep water wave scenarios. Despite this, deriving exact solutions remains a complex task due to its coupled nature. A simplified approach emerges when reducing the equation to a radial heat equation on a semi-infinite domain with boundary conditions that involve the wave's spatial derivative and amplitude. However, the relationship between these derivatives and amplitudes grows arbitrarily large as one moves away from the boundary, making the domain effectively one-dimensional. In this reduced setting, we examine the behavior of the wave's amplitude and its spatial derivative as governed by an oscillator-like equation, where an analytical expression for the reflection coefficient is developed when a wave with finite amplitude and its spatial derivative collide at a finite distance. As a result, our expression for the reflection coefficient exhibits a significant, non-intuitive, linear relationship with the wave number. This unique behavior arises from the dispersive nature of the deep water waves, where such a linear relationship is uncharacteristic of Schrödinger-type equations. In order to support our finding, a connection is made to a recent study of the trapezoidal potential, where single and double hump versions exhibited superlinear and linear relationships between the reflection coefficient and wave number, respectively. Furthermore, in the context of complex plane scenarios, where growing and decaying solutions coexist, our derived expression for the reflection coefficient is expected to yield a significant, constant value of 1. Lastly, implications of our work are expected to extend to the original coupled DSII equation once appropriate modifications are implemented, including the introduction of a conformal map. While this extension remains the subject of ongoing research, our analysis provides an interesting link between the original equation and a modified version of the Schrödinger equation in a non-linear fashion. In the course of our investigation, a number of interesting non-linear relationships between the two equations became apparent, where key solutions were found via direct integration rather than variational methods. In order to rectify this shortcoming, our research is expected to pave the way for the development of new approaches to collision theory in the future. Several advanced text categorization algorithms have been developed but many existing datasets have not been thoroughly examined for their consistency in categorization tasks. Traditional methods often overlook the effects of missing attributes in documents, assuming all features are equally relevant. We present Sibylvars, a set of variant mapping functions that can be utilized to modify any given background classifier, making a system immune to specific words during categorization tasks. We apply this modified Variants approach to several existing categorization algorithms and test its effectiveness on different datasets. Experiments conducted with Reuters and Genomic Functional Category datasets show that Sibylvars enhances the robustness of these systems, achieving improved accuracy and reliability overall. Our proposed method not only outperforms existing attribute-based methods but also remedies inconsistencies in datasets like Reuters that have been identified as being caused by specific missing attributes. Sibylvars enables a dynamic and efficient way to overcome inherent limitations of all current background categorization methods that were inherently prone to missing attributes. Sibylvars allows for an automatic and seamless modification of any current background categorization algorithm making it more robust, efficient, and reliable. Training times are substantially reduced, efficient and reliable compared to traditional Attribute Selection methods. We propose a new evaluation metric to assess the inherent robustness of any given categorization algorithm. We propose a new paradigm, called Parallel Categorization Assessment (PCA), to independently test the effectiveness of any given categorization method. Utilizing the Sibylvars approach, we successfully demonstrate the improved robustness of several established categorization algorithms including SVM, Bagging, and Random Forest. Furthermore, we successfully apply the Sibylvars approach to the established French dataset which was previously considered as a fixed background marking. We successfully demonstrate the improved robustness of several established categorization algorithms including Maximal Margin Assigner. The results of our experiments show a considerable and consistent improvement in accuracy and robustness metrics for the Sibylvars method in both intrinsic and extrinsic evaluations on the French dataset. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results in both intrinsic and extrinsic evaluations on the French dataset. The methodology and proposed resources, including source code and datasets, are made publicly available for replication purposes. The objective of meta-learning is to prepare a model that can quickly learn
new tasks with minimal supervision. Typically, researchers train these models
using multiple diverse tasks to achieve this goal, however, our study presents
a framework where a model can rapidly learn new tasks with minimal requirements
of data and hyperparameter tuning. We propose a system where a student neural
network observes the effects of various weights to rapidly learn new tasks with
minimal supervision and confidently eliminate incorrect options. Experimental
results show that our basic model is effective in reducing the time needed to
solve a problem from around 100 seconds to around 2 seconds, we have also shown
that our basic model is nearly as effective as a highly optimised state of the
art model that was trained on thousands of different tasks to achieve this
goal, Additionally our basic model is more interpretable than state of the art
models. One potential issue that was discovered during testing was that the
model sometimes spends too much time weighing all the different options this
causes a delay in time to solve a problem, however our team has come up with a
number of methods to mitigate this problem including the use of selective
strategies to reduce the number of different options to consider during a time
sensitive process. Our study offers a starting point for other researchers to
build on to develop meta-learning algorithms that are fast, efficient, and
predictive. The code for these models can be found at https://github.com/alexkusch/linear-illustrations.

Achieving resource-reduced neural machine translation models is a developing area that has seen some breakthroughs, however, a critical element remains unresolved: how to effectively decrease the models' computational demands without compromising on quality? This study investigates an unexplored area of this issue by examining the relative 'robustness' of two techniques used for small MT model development: word extraction and word quantization. We focus on some unresolved questions regarding these techniques, such as: To what extent can they be applied? Which of the two is more resistant to extreme conditions? Can we combine the advantages of both techniques? This research defines and measures 'robustness' using a novel approach that considers both translation accuracy and the consistency of the output across various techniques. We discovered that both extraction and quantization have limitations, but in different areas: extraction produces inconsistent outputs if the number of words used is too small or too large. On the other hand, quantization results in a decline in translation accuracy if the number of quantization levels used is too large or too small. This study also reveals that both techniques can build robust low-resource MT models, but to a varying degree: word extraction leads to a translation accuracy boost of around 4-10%, whereas word quantization achieves a boost of around 1-4%. To increase the translation accuracy of both techniques, we investigated different strategies to combine them, and discovered that mixing extraction and quantization can bring about a trade-off between both approaches, increasing the overall translation accuracy by as much as 5%. This study demonstrates that both techniques can be utilized to develop lightweight MT models. We deliver the source code for our study at https://github.com/multinlp/mt_extr_quant_. An additional demonstration of our study can be accessed at https://quicklook.net/mt-extr-quant/.

Nevertheless, extensive data annotation is required for deep learning models, which can be costly and time-consuming, especially for rare diseases. In this context, we employ noise suppression and image enhancement techniques to investigate the potential reduction of data labeling requirements for pneumonia segmentation. Our results, obtained through experiments on a small dataset of 50 images, suggest that applying denoising and image scaling can substantially decrease the need for labeled data, enabling high-quality segmentation even with a substantially reduced dataset. Voice translation is a complex task that involves translating spoken words into target languages without prior knowledge of the target languages. Existing voice translation systems typically require users to be familiar with the target languages, making them ineffective for languages where users have little to no understanding. This paper explores a variant of voice translation called zero-shot voice translation, which allows users to listen to spoken dialects and have them translated into target languages without needing to establish relationships between the dialects and target languages. To accomplish this task, we developed a text-to-speech model and a speech translation model that can learn the translation of spoken dialects and foreign languages respectively, then combined the two models with a control flow mechanism to facilitate zero-shot voice translation. Our research shows that our approach can effectively translate speech across multiple languages. When tested on a two-stage translation task from English into Mandarin, Romanized Mandarin, Spanish, Portuguese and German, it achieved a high translation accuracy of 75.2%, outperforming the baseline model with a significant difference of 19.7%. Our research also demonstrates the effectiveness of the text-to-speech model in creating fake audio recordings of given translations, and the translation accuracy can be further improved if the speech model's performance is enhanced. This breakthrough has the potential to facilitate global communication and make languages more accessible. Our research opens a new door to enabling voice translation without prior knowledge of the target languages, and future studies can build upon our work to translate speech into more languages, expanding its applications to more scenarios. We develop new dynamic boundary conditions, establish their well-posedness, and prove the unique solutions to the resulting partial differential equations are smooth. Furthermore, we extend the theory to its nonlinear form and explore its connection with a nonlinear Stefan problem involving mass loss. A key aspect of our research is the development of a linearization result, which enables the analysis of stability near equilibrium states even under the stringent dynamic boundary conditions. Our work also reveals an intriguing connection between the linearized equations and a specific class of elliptic equations. Finally, we demonstrate the importance of considering boundary conditions that account for material dissipation in fluids undergoing phase changes. The results of this research are presented in a series of papers, which will be made available on the arXiv repository. The first paper explores the well-posedness of a vast class of parabolic equations, while the second delves into the free-boundary problems associated with these systems. The existing manuscript focuses on the development of a comprehensive framework for deriving correct and effective mathematical models of heat flow with dynamic boundaries. By recognizing the limitations of existing theories, particularly those of Coleman and Gurtin, we embark on a mission to establish a systematic approach for writing heat flow equations that are compatible with dynamic boundaries. We achieve this goal by introducing the concept of admissible functions, which lays the foundation for our theory's success. Our research enables the derivation of unique, non-problematic heat flow equations, which is facilitated by the introduction of a divergence theorem that is applicable to arbitrary domains. These findings are then applied to derive new formulae for the Laplace operator with dynamic boundaries, which serve as a crucial component of our theory. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the resulting equations can be viewed as a natural extension of the classical Laplace equation, which is a fundamental aspect of mathematical physics. Significant shifts are occurring in the way districts are used, which is causing variations in load demand during the day. As a result, the low voltage electricity network is experiencing increased stress, and delivering efficient service requires considering the unique characteristics of this sector. Studies on forecasting are largely focused on high voltage networks, but there's a need for improved forecasting tools that integrate load data and provide accurate predictions, which can be achieved by fusing predictions in a probabilistic way. This fusion enables predictions to be based on a geostatistical model that considers the spatial relationships of subareas within a district as well as their connections, while also taking into account the unpredictability of daily changes in load demand. This approach involves three key elements: (i) district-level predictions generated through hierarchical statistical models that consider local tendencies and characteristics, (ii) short-term predictions that consider daily fluctuations, and (iii) short-term predictions that consider external factors such as weather, pointing out a need for additional research on this aspect. This approach was tested using actual data from a Italian district served by the low voltage Molena LTspider network. Specifically, predictions were made for the neighborhood of Milan, which was divided into five areas. By comparing predictions with actual values, we found that the fusion of predictions in a probabilistic way significantly improves the accuracy of our forecasts. Moreover, these predictions are not just limited to aggregate load demand but also consider the variability of daily changes in load. This not only helps ensure a reliable supply of energy but also reduces the impact of variations in load demand during the day. Finally, these predictions were used to calculate daily peak load predictions, which were found to significantly improve by more than 30% when predictions are made for five areas of the district rather than the district as a whole. Additionally, predictions made at the single area level have also shown improvements of at least 70%. These results not only demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach but also suggest the need for further research, which should consider the impact of weather on predictions. Potential areas for this research could be developing advanced models that integrate weather and non weather-related factors, which may involve a more thorough analysis of consumption patterns. One such possible factor could be the impact of residential consumption, which may be influenced by a variety of factors, including demographic components, such as population density, which may in turn affect load demand. Another potential area for this research could be the integration of other significant factors such as industrial consumption, which may have a more pronounced impact due to the limited number of industrial consumers in a district

Using an expert elicitation case study, we demonstrate the application of our framework in real-world scenarios. Accurate diagnosis of COVID-19, particularly when symptoms are not prominent, heavily relies on chest X-ray analyses by healthcare professionals to determine if patients should be isolated. Current methods employ deep learning techniques, specifically semantic segmentation, to identify respiratory issues in these X-rays. However, typical approaches require large datasets annotated by experts, which is impractical and costly due to the time involved. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an innovative framework that utilizes weakly labeled datasets for both segmentation and detection of COVID-19 related lesions in chest X-rays. This framework, consisting of two main components, leverages two types of annotations: outline-based masks and categorical labels for a more efficient data preparation process. The results show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on two public datasets, with notable successes on both precision and recall metrics. Additionally, we make our source code freely available for further research. Verification experiments using the COCO-pancreas dataset have also confirmed its effectiveness, providing evidence that our proposed framework is adaptable to other computer-aided diagnosis applications. The performance of our approach is impressive, with high recall and moderate loss in precision compared to methods using fully annotated datasets, offering an efficient solution for localizing and segmenting respiratory lesions in chest X-rays using weakly guided learning. Vertebral fractures are a significant public health concern, especially among older adults, due to their association with mobility limitations and even mortality risks. As such, accurate vertebral structure analysis is crucial, but manually contouring each vertebra is time-consuming and error-prone. To streamline this process, researchers have developed automated vertebral contouring techniques using CT scans, although many current approaches rely on optimized templates or features derived from typical vertebra shapes, which can be problematic due to variations in vertebral anatomy. To address these challenges, a novel method is proposed that incorporates a vertebrasegmentation component and an anatomically constrained optimization technique to localize and identify vertebrae more effectively. This method involves a spine rectification step to improve 3D reconstruction and enhance visualization, and a optimization framework that accounts for anatomical differences and promotes more realistic vertebrapositions. In a comparison with standard approaches, results suggest that the new method localizes vertebrae more accurately, contours vertebral shapes more precisely, and yields fewerskeleton errors, and even to the best of authors' knowledge,this method offers the most comprehensive and effective vertebralocalization and recognition capabilities. In situations where data is limited, these problems become known as ill-posed problems. A particular approach to solving these problems is dual gradient descent, which has been effective in several contexts. This method can be applied to problems with measurements constrained within specific ranges as well as those with certain types of noise. Although it has been successful, this approach has some limitations, such as being sensitive to conditions that are difficult to control. In order to expand the range of applicable conditions, an improved dual gradient descent algorithm is proposed, which has more general requirements and is therefore more versatile. This algorithm can be used to solve a range of problems, from those with noisy measurements to those with noisy solutions. A significant challenge in estimating the depth from a light field is the occurrence of occlusions, particularly in the cross-spectral dimension, which hampers the recovery of occluded areas. We have found that patches from the same object that are hidden behind another object in one patch are likely to be hidden in another patch, which enables us to design a novel cost function that excels in detecting the disunity of occluded patches. Additionally, our cost function outperforms other state-of-the-art methods by effectively utilizing periodic patterns in light fields, which are prevalent in areas with missing information, thus providing a reliable hint for discovering the central patch. We have further refined our approach by considering the multi-modal context of light fields, combining our proposed cost function with an existing deep learning method that leverages structural information, which significantly enhances the estimation quality. We have extensively tested our approach on various light field datasets, which has resulted in superior performance compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods, with particular improvement in areas with significant occlusions. The Fokas-Lenells equation, an extension of the Hirota equation, has been investigated using the bilinear method. New solutions have been discovered and verified, including mult-soliton solutions whose properties are well-documented. Further study involved examining collision events among the solutions. As an alternative to the Fokas-Lenells equation, a new system of equations was also presented in integrated form. This system is equivalent to the Fokas-Lenells equation in quadrature and provides a means of accessing its rich solution set via the Fokas-Lenells formulas. Notably, for two-soliton interactions of the new system, specific resonant conditions were identified, and corresponding multiquadron and dark-soliton solutions were derived. Moreover, for non-resonant conditions, solutions in the form of rational solutions and solutions possessing high irregularity were found through the bilinear approach. Lastly, interesting periodic solutions of the Fokas-Lenells equation were discovered by combining the solutions of the Lenells equation with high irregularity and a specific periodic extension of the Fokas-Lenells equation. This research demonstrates that the bilinear method offers an effective approach to investigating the solution set of the Fokas-Lenells equation and facilitates discovery of novel solutions. However, for theories relying on the hyperbolic heat equation, the continuum formulation appears to be unattainable. Consequently, the solutions derived in this research primarily serve illustrative purposes for the integrable nature of the Fokas-Lenells equation. Nevertheless, it is hypothesized that the continuum of the solutions of the Fokas-Lenells equation may be useful in developing new numerical methods, known as admissable numerical methods, for solving the Fokas-Lenells equation. That is to say, if a set of solutions for a given time T is found, then any function with a similar profile to these solutions can be employed as an admissible numerical method in a way that is to a certain extent arbitrarily precise. In the increasingly prevalent, densely-installed home WiFi networks, the addition of new access points is often suggested to ensure optimal network performance. Before making this decision, however, it's essential to assess the impact on existing infrastructure, which can be achieved by gathering detailed network data through the ongoing connectivity review process in IEEE 802.11k/v standards. Our proposal suggests utilizing the collected data to simulate and evaluate the performance improvement of adding new access points or extending existing ones within the network. In this study, we demonstrate the feasibility of adopting this methodical approach by collecting usage metrics, channel analysis, and simulation-based evaluation to make informed decisions about network architecture. Our case study involves measuring and simulating home WiFi networks consisting of up to five floors and delivering crucial metrics to support technical assessments and performance optimization decisions. By applying the proposed method, network administrators can effectively choose the best configuration for adding new access points or extending existing ones, ultimately leading to enhanced network performance and efficiency. Our comprehensive evaluation, fueled by extensive real-world data collection, confirms that the proposed technique not only reduces interference but also improves overall network performance and durability. In particular, we have identified that adding new extension nodes instead of new access points can help mitigate channel congestion and thus, contribute to a more efficient and durable network infrastructure. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the problem of channel load is more pronounced during evening hours, implying a potential correlation between the time of day and network performance, which could potentially be optimized by adjusting configuration settings accordingly. Ultimately, to further optimize network performance, we propose the IEEE 802.11k/v based auto-configuration feature, allowing the review process to suggest the most beneficial configuration based on the network evaluation results. The proposal is implemented using the existing IEEE 802.11k/v standards on the MDKU tool, which enables us to gather crucial network data within a realistic time frame for efficient configuration optimization. In particular, our implementation reveals that the proposed technique can provide a useful insight into optimizing network performance, namely by suggesting the most beneficial configuration based on the evaluation results. One notable limitation of our proposal is that the IEEE 802.11k/v standards can only gather data for up to two hours before the connection review process is initiated.
